How to clean a stainless steel sink and bring back its showroom shine using basic cupboard staples

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you are getting your home ready for festive hosting, do not overlook the sink. Even with pristine worktops and clean floors, cloudy stainless steel covered in chalky water rings instantly makes a kitchen feel tired.

Before the holiday cooking frenzy begins, you can revive a dull basin without scratching the metal or buying pricey specialty cleaners. This five-minute routine cuts through greasy buildup and seals in a bright, showroom shine just in time for visitors.

Rinse away loose food debris, then wash the entire basin thoroughly with hot water and dish soap. Using a soft microfiber cloth or non-scratch sponge, wipe in long, steady strokes that follow the faint brushed grain of the steel rather than scrubbing in circles.

This removes the surface grease film so your cleaning paste can make direct contact with the mineral spots underneath.

Sprinkle a light dusting of baking soda over the damp steel, concentrating on the drain and faucet base where hard water residue gathers. Using a damp cloth, work the powder into a paste along the metal's grain to lift dull water rings without scratching.

For stubborn hard-water marks, rinse the baking soda paste away thoroughly first, then apply a light spray of white vinegar directly to the mineral scale.

Letting the vinegar sit undiluted for a few minutes allows its mild acetic acid to chemically dissolve crusty calcium and magnesium deposits without being neutralized by the alkaline baking soda.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Avoid spraying vinegar onto specialized faucet finishes like matte black, brass, or oil-rubbed bronze, as the acid can strip or discolor the coating.

Once the mineral scale softens, use a soft-bristled brush or non-scratch sponge to gently agitate and lift any remaining gritty buildup from the metal’s surface texture.

Standing water left to evaporate is why cloudy spots return. Use a dry dish towel or microfiber cloth to wipe the entire basin, faucet, and drainboard until completely dry.

For an optional finishing shine, apply a single drop of mineral oil (like baby oil) or olive oil to a soft cloth and buff it into the steel, following the direction of the metal's grain. Buff vigorously with a clean, dry section of the towel until no residue remains.

This creates a light barrier that repels water beads and keeps the shine lasting longer, especially on faucets and handles.

#3417. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

#3416. Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

From the misty seaports of Massachusetts seaports to the otherworldly town of Twin Peaks and even the distant shores of Troy, Ruth De Jong has spent the past twenty years transporting audiences into the unforgettable worlds created by auteur directors like Paul Thomas Anderson, Terrence Malick, Kenneth Lonergan, David Lynch, Jordan Peele, and Christopher Nolan.

“My goal in my work is to always paint the most authentic pictures,” De Jong shared with IndieWire at the Virginia Film Festival, where the production designer received the festival’s Craft Award. The town of Charlottesville has a special place in De Jong’s heart.

It’s here where legendary production designer Jack Fisk, father of De Jong’s high school friend Schuyler Fisk, suggested she forgo attending the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts for grad school in favor of working on the set of Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2007 Oscar-winning film “There Will Be Blood” instead. Recalling that fateful conversation, De Jong said that Fisk told her he saw the younger version of himself in her, sharing, “I think what the world continually needs are mentors [like Fisk] showing up.” Related Stories IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

De Jong fell in love with filmmaking as she continued to work with Fisk on Anderson’s “The Master,” and a handful of films by Terence Malick, including his Palme d’Or winner “The Tree of Life.” Eventually she spread her wings and took on her first film as production designer: Kenneth Lonergan’s “Manchester by the Sea.” Looking back on these early days and everything she learned on those sets, De Jong said that she believes “a body of work like that is built upon itself. I think I’m constantly pulling from the past, but also pulling from the future.”

Whether designing a fishing village in modern-day Gloucester, recreating the White House Oval Office, or crafting the iconic Trojan horse, all of De Jong’s work comes in service of the characters and story being told. While crafting a film’s world, De Jong asks herself, “How do I make this tangible and alive and real and authentic?”

To capture undertones of the real working-class people in the fishing community at the center of “Manchester by the Sea,” this meant spending time with local fishermen. “We asked if we could go into their houses. We asked if we could use their fishing boats. We asked if we could use their lobster cages and rope everything, and then we would,” De Jong recalled. All of this research helped De Jong nail the subtle nuances and layers of the region. “You’re always striving to not make it cliché,” De Jong told IndieWire.

The first step involves breaking down the script. At this phase of her process, De Jong attaches an image to each scene. “It may be a piece of art. It could be a photograph. It could be a texture. It could be a piece of cloth. It could be anything,” she shared, adding, “Then from that, I add physical locations, and we start putting the whole thing together and seeing our film.”

Sometimes these images come from the director themselves. While working on “Twin Peaks: The Return,” David Lynch gave De Jong some of his own artwork for inspiration. “He would hand me some of his paintings, his drawings, his work, and say, ‘Here, this is this set. Build that,,’” De Jong revealed, adding that even if it was “a flat 2D painting, the colors were wild and it’s textural.” These came in handy for the new worlds of the series, like the landmark Episode 8 (also known as “Gotta Light?”), in which De Jong designed the radio station and other eerier riffs on the atomic age 1950s.

For the more iconic aspects of “Twin Peaks, ” De Jong also dug up the original plans for the Red Room from the 1990s. “David remembered in his mind’s eye,” De Jong said, “and I’m there to continue to be David’s conduit on the new work. It was just a beautiful, beautiful dance.”

Along with reviving iconic sets from pop culture’s past, De Jong herself has created work that has become part of the entertainment firmament. The set she created for the “Jupiter’s Claim” theme park in Jordan Peele’s “Nope” has been added to the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, a unique feat for an aspect of filmmaking that is often binned as soon as a production wraps. On the honor of her set being preserved in such a way, De Jong said, “It’s pretty incredible, because in the act of doing it, you aren’t thinking about what this is going to turn into.”

After receiving her first Oscar nomination for her work on Christopher Nolan‘s Best Picture-winning biopic “Oppenheimer,” De Jong re-teamed with the writer-director this year for his ambitious take on Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” For this film, her process began at Nolan’s home, where she spent hours reading the script. Afterwards, De Jong asked for the parameters. “He said, ‘There are none,'” De Jong recalled.

This allowed the designer the freedom to “take the audience on the same journey that Odysseus (Matt Damon) was on,” she said. Starting with seven countries, De Jong and Nolan began searching for the film’s faraway locations, the only edict being that Nolan wanted the film to start in the Mediterranean and end in the Mediterranean. Without the barriers of realism, De Jong found inspiration in locations across the globe. “We didn’t care that we were shooting the Laestrygonians in Scotland. It didn’t matter. It just had the topography we were interested in. Same with Iceland and the same with Morocco,” De Jong said. Once the locations were determined, then came building sets that reflected the characters who inhabit them.

For the ominous stone house owned by Circe (Samantha Morton), who beguiles Odysseus’ men and turns them into pigs, De Jong shared that Nolan “was very clear about not wanting Circe’s home to be a Hansel and Gretel in the woods type cottage. She’s so peculiar and unique and bizarre and a witch.” With this in mind, the duo decided she should live on the edge of a cliff, finding the perfect craggy rocks in Scotland. Soon, a whole backstory informed the building of her dwelling. “She formed her house out of those craggy rocks,” De Jong said, adding, “We just made up all these stories and created the sets from there.”

The same attention to character informed the creation of the iconic Trojan horse, an imposing image of which opens the epic film. Nolan envisioned a rearing horse, telling De Jong that “it has to be iconic and it has to be larger than life.” For Nolan, De Jong said, the question at the center of this opening scene is, “Are the Trojans going to accept the gift?” Thinking about what kind of horse would be accepted, Nolan wanted their horse to be “the antithesis” of the one in Wolfgang Petersen’s 2004 film “Troy.” “We didn’t want the clunky wheels,” she said, adding that “these were master shipbuilders.”

“They’re master craftsmen,” De Jong insists, “If they collected all this wood, why don’t we shiplap the entire body, shiplap the tail? They hand-carved the legs and the head. That leaves the body all hollow like a ship, so all the men could all go inside and cut a trap door.” Once they agreed on the backstory for the building of the horse, the next step was figuring out how to make multiples out of fiberglass (and later out of plastic as one of the summer’s hottest collectible popcorn buckets).

As “The Odyssey” marches its way into awards season, De Jong is looking towards her future – and her next gig. With every project she takes, De Jong is looking to push herself as an artist. “It’s that space of being uncomfortable that is how you know you’re in the right place,” she said, adding, “The minute I find comfort, I realize I’m in the wrong place. So I’m always pushing to get back into that area of discomfort.”

Thinking back to her conversation with Fisk all those years ago, De Jong feels that what he taught her was “The act of physically doing and going and staying in momentum,” adding, “That’s something that Christopher Nolan has. All of these directors; They don’t stop producing work. They don’t do it in vain. They do it because that’s their language and their medium. They’re all artists at heart.”

Although De Jong looks back at her past fondly, she doesn’t regret forgoing art school to join the movie business. What she learned after all these years is that, “You need to go forward, and even if you go forward and you hit a wall, then just keep pivoting a little bit. Stay open and don’t be fearful. You can’t fear. I’d rather screw up royally and have tried than not tried at all.”

#3413. Marvel Officially Debuts New Avengers Movie on Disney+ Today

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

After three hours of watching the Avengers try to undo what Thanos did, the last thing Avengers: Endgame gives us is a dance in somebody’s living room. Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) finally gets to be with Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell), and for a few seconds, nobody needs Captain America for anything. The Russo Brothers went back to that scene seven years later and added a knock at the door.

When Marvel brought Endgame back to theaters in September, audiences got to see who was on the other side of that door. There was more waiting in the credits, too, including a sound anyone who’s seen the first Iron Man might recognize before they realize whose face they’re looking at. Fans who saw the re-release in IMAX or an Infinity Vision-certified theater also got a separate sneak peek at Avengers: Doomsday.

Marvel Studios’ Avengers Endgame: Encore is now streaming exclusively on Disney+. The extended cut arrived on the streaming platform today, November 13, with updated color grading and about four minutes of new footage connecting the 2019 movie to Avengers: Doomsday. Disney+ confirms the added scenes are included in the streaming release. The premium-format sneak peek was advertised separately for theaters.

Four villains, and four arguments the films were honest enough to actually let them make. Here is the one you lean towards, the part of it that holds up, and the exact point where it stops holding up.

You align with the one who was right about the problem and wrong about the solution. Killmonger is the most persuasive villain Marvel has produced because the film never pretends his anger came from nowhere.

You align with the protector, which is the most understandable and most dangerous position on this list. Namor is not chasing power or revenge, he is doing whatever keeps his people hidden, and he has been doing it for centuries.

You align with the patient one, the only man on this list with no powers, no army and no hurry. Zemo lost his family in Sokovia and then spent years working out that you do not fight the Avengers, you introduce them to each other's secrets.

You align with the one who decided the answer was arithmetic. Thanos is not angry and not grieving in any way he will admit to, he simply reached a conclusion and never once revisited it, which is precisely what makes him frightening.

Spoilers for the new Encore footage follow.When Peggy answers the door, it’s Tom Hiddleston’s Loki. He tells her he can help both of them, and “both” is the part audiences keep coming back to. Steve spent years trying to get back to Peggy, and the first person to interrupt their dance makes his pitch to her. It’s an especially good use of Loki, whose own second chance came courtesy of the Avengers’ time heist. They gave him an opening to grab the Tesseract and run, setting his Disney+ series in motion. Now he’s on the doorstep of the life Steve went back in time to have.

The first credits scene picks up with Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner after Spider-Man: Brand New Day. He’s recording himself in an underground bunker, explaining how he plans to keep the Hulk under control when the feed glitches. Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom speaks from off-screen. There’s a flash of green, the Hulk roars, and a magical sigil is all that’s left in the cell. At the TVA, Mobius, Casey, and O.B. watch the Fox X-Men universe and another Earth fire missiles at each other as they collide. The alerts keep coming, and the count of lost universes climbs into the thousands.

Then comes the sound of Tony Stark hammering out his first Iron Man mask. That’s a hell of a sound to hear at the end of Endgame, especially with Downey Jr. back in the picture. You know whose face you expect to see, but this time, the last face the movie leaves you with is Doom’s.

Avengers Endgame: Encore is streaming on Disney+. Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters December 18.

#3411. 30-Episode Netflix Action Thriller Series Cracked The Code For Book Adaptations

While Netflix’s action thriller series managed to pull off an incredible feat when it comes to page-to-screen adaptation, the streaming service doesn’t have a replacement for the show after its upcoming series finale. It is never easy to adapt a book to TV, whether creators are dealing with elaborate magic systems like SyFy’s The Magicians or complex in-universe worldbuilding, as was the case for Prime Video’s Lord of the Rings prequel The Rings of Power.

Even outside the lore-heavy worlds of fantasy and sci-fi, thriller novel adaptations can struggle just as much with their transition to the screen. Characters like Karin Slaughter’s Will Trent or Michael Connelly’s iconic detective Harry Bosch are lone wolves who don’t work well with others in their source novels, but the shows Will Trent and Bosch needed to alter this character detail so the strong, silent title characters would actually have some dialogue and character relationships.

However, the biggest challenge for screen adaptations of books always comes when shows run out of existing literary source material. Hulu’s dystopian show The Handmaid’s Tale faithfully adapted author Margaret Atwood’s novel in its first season, and spent the remaining five seasons telling an original story that expanded on the plot of the iconic book with new material. Similarly, Netflix’s The Night Agent lasted three successful seasons even after running out of source material.

Based on author Matthew Quirk’s 2019 novel of the same name, The Night Agent season 1 introduced Gabriel Basso’s conflicted FBI agent Peter Sutherland as he investigates a mole within the US government. The show’s first outing was a massive hit for Netflix, joining Prime Video’s The Terminal List, Hanna, Citadel, and Mr. & Mrs. Smith to become part of the streaming era’s spy show resurgence.

However, there was another series that The Night Agent garnered even more comparisons to. With its irredeemably evil villains, fast-paced action, and escapist feel, The Night Agent was frequently called a masterpiece of “Dad TV” alongside Prime Video’s iconic Reacher franchise. The big difference was that every season of Reacher adapted a different book from author Lee Child’s extensive, ongoing novel series of the same name, whereas The Night Agent ran out of source material at the end of season 1.

Fortunately, The Night Agent seasons 2 and 3 not only managed to overcome this, but even earned better reviews than their predecessor when the show moved on from its original inspiration. With a shared Rotten Tomatoes critical rating of 86% compared to season 1’s 75%, The Night Agent was a hit with viewers even though the show now had to come up with its own storylines on the fly.

Sadly, all good things must come to an end and, rather than trying to drag the show out for as long as possible, Netflix opted to cancel The Night Agent after its upcoming fourth and final season. Compared to the Reacher franchise’s recent expansion, this pragmatic but unfortunate choice makes sense, since The Night Agent is more likely to struggle without any source material after a full two seasons of original stories.

However, while Prime Video had Reacher in the proverbial chamber after the streaming service canceled their earlier Tom Clancy adaptation Jack Ryan, Netflix doesn’t have a similarly crowd-pleasing thriller franchise ready to replace The Night Agent. Although Netflix does have Black Doves, that darkly funny British spy series is closer in tone to Apple TV’s comparatively grounded Slow Horses than The Night Agent.

When it comes to purely fun, fast-paced action thrillers, Netflix risks lagging behind Prime Video thanks to Reacher’s popularity. Thus, the ending of The Night Agent is both well advised and, simultaneously, somewhat ill-time for the streaming service.

There's quite a bit of variety here, too, from battery-powered projectors you can take camping or move between rooms to more powerful 4K models designed for a dedicated movie-night setup.

The Soundcore Nebula P1i is down to $299 from $399, while the Nebula P1 is $699.99, down from $799. Both offer 1080p resolution and Google TV, but their speaker setups are what make them interesting. The P1i has two 10W speakers that flip out and rotate to direct sound toward your seating area, while the P1's speakers detach completely and can run wirelessly for up to 20 hours. The P1 is also brighter at 650 ANSI lumens versus the P1i's 380, though you'll need a power outlet for either projector since neither has a built-in battery.

Small enough to slip into a bag, the Nebula Capsule 3 and Capsule 3 Laser are worth considering if you want something you can easily take on trips or move around the house. The standard Capsule 3 is down to $399 from $529, saving you $130, while the Laser version is $649.99, down from $749.99. Both offer 1080p resolution, automatic image adjustments, and up to 2.5 hours of battery life, although the Laser model is a little brighter at 300 ANSI lumens compared with the standard model's 200.

Taking movie night outdoors is a little easier with a battery-powered projector, and both the Nebula Mars 3 Air and Mars 3 are designed for just that. The smaller Mars 3 Air is down to $519.99 from $599.99, offering 1080p resolution, 400 ANSI lumens of brightness, and up to 2.5 hours of playback. The larger Mars 3, now $899.99 from $999.99, steps things up with 1,000 ANSI lumens, up to five hours of battery life in Eco mode, and a more powerful 40W speaker. It also has a weather-resistant design that's useful for camping or backyard screenings, though its extra bulk might make it less convenient to carry around.

If you're ready to move beyond 1080p, the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE at $1,099.99 (originally $1,299.99) offers a more affordable way to get 4K resolution. Its hybrid LED and laser light source delivers up to 1,800 ANSI lumens, while its Dolby Vision support helps bring out more detail in compatible movies and shows. You also get Google TV and automatic image adjustments for easier setup, though it doesn't have a built-in battery, so you'll need a power outlet nearby.

At the premium end of Nebula's lineup, the X1 and newer X1S are designed for a more serious home theater setup. The X1 is down to $2,299 from $2,999, saving you $700, while the X1S is $2,799 from $3,299. Both use triple-laser technology with 4K resolution, Dolby Vision, and optical zoom, but the X1S has a considerable advantage in brightness, reaching up to 6,000 ANSI lumens compared with the X1's 3,500. That extra brightness is useful in rooms with some ambient light, but the tradeoff is louder fan noise.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3409. 7 Sci-Fi Masterpieces Goodreads Readers Love More Than ‘Dune’

That is an incendiary-sounding headline, so at the risk of getting defensive too quickly, let’s get some things in line and explain it. If you're skimming and scrolling already, then you're a lost cause, and you're already not reading, so whatever. That’s funny. You find an article about books and you don’t read any of it. Anyway… sci-fi books better than Dune? Really? No! Well, probably no. Dune is a fantastic book, and even if you don’t love it for whatever reason, you can likely, at the very least, admire what it’s done for science fiction, as a genre.

If you go on Goodreads, it has an impressive average rating, at 4.29/5, but there are a few well-known sci-fi books that have higher ratings, and some of them are below. That’s the metric. It’s to do with average ratings on Goodreads. It’s not a guarantee, by any means, that everyone on Goodreads feels these sci-fi books are better than the original Dune, but for whatever reason (or reasons, maybe sometimes some potentially understandable ones), they are rated higher. Do with that what you will, and please don’t shoot the messenger.

You're probably better off pretending Ender’s Game is one of those books that hasn’t received some kind of adaptation, since there aren’t a whole heap of positive things that can be said about the movie of the same name that came out in 2013. But hey, the book’s the book, and having the source material feel superior isn't exactly uncommon. The reception on Goodreads reflects that, because it’s got a 4.31/5 on there.

Also, Ender’s Game has more than 1.5 million ratings, and something you find when it comes to books with tons of ratings is that the average rating can be a bit lower than expected. Like, certain heavy-hitters like Nineteen Eighty-Four, Fahrenheit 451, and Slaughterhouse-Five don’t rank as highly as Dune, maybe because some people rating it feel those books are overrated. And sure, maybe some people on Goodreads still find Ender’s Game and Dune overrated, but probably not as many.

Apologies in advance to anyone who’s not a huge Andy Weir fan, but the people of Goodreads are, at least when it comes to two of his books. The first of those two books worth mentioning is Project Hail Mary, which is about an astronaut on a spacecraft on his own, and he doesn’t entirely remember how he got there. But he slowly learns, as does the reader, and his mission out in space turns out to be a high-stakes one, to say the least.

At the time of writing, it has nearly 2 million ratings on Goodreads, and the average rating is at a 4.51/5.

That might make Project Hail Mary sound quite intense, but it’s also very entertaining, since it does some interesting things structurally while ultimately being quite hard to fault as far as pacing is concerned. At the time of writing, it has nearly 2 million ratings on Goodreads, and the average rating is at a 4.51/5. It cannot claim to have the cultural legacy or significance of Dune, by any means, but hey, people who've read it have generally seemed to really love it, so that’s worth something.

The Stand falls a little short of being the highest-rated Stephen King book on Goodreads, but then again, it’s second only to The Green Mile, and that definitely counts for something when you're looking at an author with as many published novels as King. Regarding The Stand specifically, it’s a bit of a blend of genres, though one of them is possibly science fiction, or at least that’s one of the genres it belongs to on Goodreads, so there you go, and here The Stand is.

Maybe it’s easy to define as a dark fantasy book, sure. It’s got the whole end of the world thing going for it, which is post-apocalyptic, and post-apocalyptic books are generally sci-fi, but the conflict here does, before too long, lean into some pretty intense supernatural/horror territory. The Stand is frightening, then, in many ways, but that’s also to be expected with King. Look, it’s a long book (especially the uncut version from 1990). It’s hard to summarize. But it is immense, and it is very much deserving of a 4.35/5 rating, which is what it’s sitting at on Goodreads currently.

This one might seem alarming, and once more, it has to be stressed that the messenger shouldn’t be shot, but the first The Hunger Games book is beloved in general, and particularly so on Goodreads. It sits at 4.36/5 on there, so here it sits at #4 here, within this particular ranking. It struck a chord. People dug it. And it does have a higher rating than some books in long-running young adult series of this rough generation… certainly more than Twilight, though a little shy of the rating for the first Harry Potter book.

Sure, they're works of fantasy, so all that’s a bit of a tangent, but The Hunger Games (2008) is/was iconic. Not perfect, but something that got people more interested in reading, and that’s generally worth celebrating. There are more challenging dystopian and/or sci-fi novels than this one, but if you read this when younger and it got you interested in reading more of the stuff that it might've been influenced by, that’s undeniably a good thing.

Somehow, Andy Weir returned. Returned in this ranking. He didn’t technically return with The Martian, since this one came out before Project Hail Mary and also before the one novel of his that doesn’t have that much love on Goodreads (2017’s Artemis, which sits at a 3.67/5 rating). It’s worth highlighting some of the similarities with Project Hail Mary and The Martian, though, because the latter is also largely about one guy having to do quite a lot on his own.

Sure, that’s not a perfect description of Project Hail Mary, given some of the things that are revealed as it goes along, and The Martian has a bit more going on than just one man trying to stay alive in space, yet the similarities are there. It’s not hard to see how these two novels were written by the same person, but Weir does this kind of science fiction well, and so The Martian sitting at 4.42/5 on Goodreads feels pretty deserved. It is an easy-to-like book, after all.

Okay, when The Stand was mentioned before as having the second-highest rating of a Stephen King book, it’s a little more complicated, since 11/22/63 also sits at a 4.35/5. It’s more of a science fiction novel, for what that’s worth, since the premise involves time travel and the plot concerns someone going back in time to try to prevent the assassination of John F. Kennedy, hoping that getting to the bottom of said event and stopping it will positively impact everything that happens after the titular date.

Complications do ensue, and also, the method of time traveling is far from convenient, since the protagonist can only go back to 1958, and has to navigate life in the past while waiting for the inevitable. Stephen King gets a whole lot of tension out of the high-concept premise here, with the start of 11/22/63 being great, the ending being one of the author’s best, and then everything in between also being amazing. If anything, 4.35/5 could be a tad low for something this good.

There is a lot in Watchmen, both by the standards of a graphic novel and any kind of non-graphic (so normal?) novel, which makes it worth putting here. It’s got a dystopian sort of thing going for it as well, and even if it’s not set in the future like a good many works of science fiction, it’s got an alternate history setting, and that alternate history has developed quite differently, as far as technology and science are concerned.

It makes for something worth rereading and analyzing, and Watchmen is also the kind of thing you can appreciate if you don’t read a lot of superhero-related stuff, but then it becomes more rewarding the more you do know (it helps with appreciating how good it is as a deconstruction). It lives up to the hype, in other words, and so the 4.39/5 rating for the compilation of all 12 volumes on Goodreads definitely makes sense.

#3408. Today’s macOS updates fix security gap involving eMudhra certificates

Apple today released macOS updates that address a security gap involving compromised eMudhra certificates, after initially blocking them in Safari, Mail, and other apps in October. Here are the details.

A few weeks ago, Mozilla reported that private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra, an Indian digital certification company, had been compromised.

In essence, these certificates are used to establish trust in digital certificates that verify website identities and enable secure connections.

With access to the compromised private keys, bad actors could potentially create fraudulent certificates that appear legitimate, allowing them to impersonate websites and intercept sensitive user information.

In response to the compromise, Apple began automatically blocking the affected certificates on October 19, followed by additional protections on October 23.

These changes were delivered through automatic certificate configuration updates, meaning users didn’t need to install a macOS update to be protected.

While these measures protected Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple’s networking and security frameworks, they didn’t cover all of macOS, as certain command-line tools, including curl and git, could still accept the compromised certificates.

At the time, Apple published a support article with instructions for administrators to manually address this remaining security gap, while promising a fix in a future macOS update.

Today, Apple updated the document to confirm that the fix is now available.

As Apple explains, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, and macOS 15.8.3, released earlier today, prevent the affected command-line tools from accepting the compromised certificates, eliminating the need for administrators to manually address the issue.

The updates also remove five root CA certificates from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, including three additional eMudhra certificates that weren’t part of Apple’s original manual workaround.

Still, for users who are unable to install the latest macOS updates, Apple continues to provide instructions for manually addressing the issue in its support document, along with the names and SHA-256 fingerprints of the 12 affected certificates and five root CA certificates removed by the updates.

Apple also notes that “some apps and tools include their own list of root CA certificates and don’t use Apple’s block or /etc/ssl/cert.pem,” and advises users to contact the developer of those apps and tools.

To read Apple’s full support document, follow this link.

#3406. Apple Intelligence completes regulatory registration for iPad and Mac in China

Apple has completed an important regulatory step ahead of Apple Intelligence’s expected launch in China this December. Here are the details.

In late October, Apple published a press release on its Chinese Newsroom website confirming its intention to launch Apple Intelligence in China this December, as part of iOS 27.3.

Apple went on to release the first iOS 27.3 developer beta a few days later, allowing users in China to test Apple Intelligence ahead of its public launch.

In its press release, however, Apple also noted that the initial rollout would be limited to iPhones, as support for other platforms was still pending regulatory approval.

Now, as spotted by Reuters, Apple Intelligence “has been ‌registered for use on tablets and laptops in China, Shanghai’s cyberspace regulator said on Monday.”

For context, generative AI services must complete a regulatory registration process before they can launch publicly in China.

Apple Intelligence, which, in China, relies on Alibaba’s Qwen model to power certain AI features, had already received regulatory approval for iPhones in July, following months of delays and negotiations with Chinese authorities.

With today’s registration, Apple has cleared another regulatory hurdle ahead of Apple Intelligence’s launch in China. However, the company has yet to confirm whether iPad and Mac support will also arrive in December.

To read Reuters‘ full report, follow this link.

#3405. 3 Best Prime Video Movies To Watch This Weekend (Nov 14-15)

November is already proving to be a popular month in theaters. As A24's viral documentary sensation, You Can See Everything, LAIKA's new animated masterpiece, Wildwood, and Olivia Colman's bonkers fantasy film Wicker continued to prove popular on the big screen last weekend, Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja's new Cat in the Hat movie and writer/director Takashi Yamazaki's Godzilla Minus Zero crashed onto the box office scene and stole the top two spots in the North American ranks. As another weekend approaches, you needn't get your movie fix with a trip to the theater. Here's a look at three Prime Video movies you should watch this weekend.

For more recommendations, check out our list of the best shows and movies on Prime Video.

Halloween might be over, but Stephen King's presence in your streaming rotation shouldn't be going anywhere. With that in mind, why not check out 2007's The Mist this weekend, based on King's 1980 novella, which was first included in the horror anthology Dark Forces. Set in the small town of Bridgton, Maine, the film follows a group of locals, including artist David Drayton (Thomas Jane), who become trapped when a sinister mist descends.

Written and directed by Frank Darabont and starring the likes of Marcia Gay Harden, Laurie Holden, Andre Braugher, and Toby Jones, this mid-noughties horror gem will chill you to your core as this politically relevant tale twists and turns towards a jaw-dropping finish. Featuring monsters designed by horror comics artist Bernie Wrightson and heaps of tension, you won't forget The Mist anytime soon.

For the perfect popcorn flick to add sparkle to your November weekend, look no further than one of the greatest adventure films of all time. Raiders of the Lost Ark, created by the winning combination of Steven Spielberg and George Lucas, stars Harrison Ford as Indiana Jones, who must race against both time and the Nazis to recover the biblical Ark of the Covenant.

Packed with typically Spielbergian ambition and heart, this iconic family favorite will never fail to brighten any weekend. One of Ford's most beloved performances features a smorgasbord of memorable moments, from the gun in a sword fight to the boulder chase. Raiders of the Lost Ark was the recipient of four Academy Awards, including Best Sound, Best Film Editing, and Best Visual Effects.

On weekends, we wear pink. This weekend, don't spend hours scrolling for what to watch when the most iconic chick flick of all time is ready and waiting for you on Prime Video. Mean Girls, written by Tina Fey and directed by Mark Waters, follows Lindsay Lohan’s Cady Heron as she joins a new school and immediately makes an impact with the A-list girl clique. However, when a mistake is made, all hell breaks loose.

Arguably one of the most quotable movies ever, Mean Girls is jam-packed with memorable moments that have been lovingly parodied countless times since. Rachel McAdams, Amanda Seyfried, Lacey Chabert, and more join Lohan in a perfectly assembled cast, as they combine to not just craft one of the best teen films of this century, but one that will forever define the genre.

#3402. Earl Thomas’ Wife Pleads Guilty to Conspiracy to Scam $2.7 Million From Ex-NFL Star

Nina Thomas -- the estranged wife of Earl Thomas -- has fallen on her sword in her criminal case, pleading guilty to conspiring to scam her former NFL star husband out of $2.7 million.

According to federal court document, obtained by TMZ, Nina will plead guilty to 1 count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud as part of a plea deal with prosecutors, and she faces a maximum of 5 years in prison and/or a $250,000 fine. The judge also ordered Nina and co-defendant Kevin Thompson to be jointly responsible for paying restitution in the amount of $3.497,444.64.

Under the agreement ... Kevin will plead guilty to 2 charges -- conspiracy to commit wire fraud and possession with intent to distribute cocaine. Kevin faces 5 years in prison on the wire fraud charge and/or a fine of $250,000. He also faces up to 40 years in prison on the cocaine distribution charge and a fine of $5 million.

As we previously reported ... in 2024, Nina and Kevin were indicted on federal charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering. Thompson was also charged with possession with intent to distribute 500 grams or more of cocaine and possession of a firearm in furtherance of a drug trafficking crime.

Prosecutors said the defendants swindled Earl out of millions of dollars after Nina’s marriage to the ex-Seattle Seahawks free safety went up in smoke.

Prosecutors alleged Nina kicked off her scheme to illegally siphon cash from Earl in September 2021 -- after she filed for divorce from him in 2020. The estranged couple got married in 2016 at a lavish ceremony attended by the likes of Russell Wilson and Ciara.

Prosecutors accuse Nina and Kevin of taking money from Earl without his knowledge ... and transferring the funds and other property into bank accounts under their control.

The authorities claim the defendants stole more than $2.7 million from the Earl ... and says they made expensive purchases, spending $28,796 on an Hermès Birkin handbag and $52,890 on a Porsche Panamera. Prosecutors also say the two charged $5,500 on Earl’s credit card for a plastic surgery operation.

Nina and Kevin were eventually arrested and taken into custody on December 16, 2024.

#3400. Canadian court certifies class action against Apple over Google search deal

A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has certified a class action against Apple over allegations that its search agreement with Google stifled competition and inflated advertising prices. Here are the details.

In recent years, Apple’s deal with Alphabet to make Google the default search engine on Safari has drawn regulatory attention in the US, the UK, and Australia, while related search competition concerns have also come under scrutiny in the EU and Japan.

While the details of each investigation differ, they all raise concerns about the impact of Google’s dominance in search, as well as the extent to which its agreements with other companies might be limiting competition.

More recently, Apple’s agreement with Google received significant attention during the US Department of Justice’s antitrust case against the search giant, which included testimony from Apple executives Eddy Cue and John Giannandrea. The latter joined Apple from Google in 2018 and led its AI efforts until stepping down earlier this year.

As a result of the US case, a federal judge ruled in August 2024 that Google had illegally maintained its monopoly in online search through anticompetitive agreements, including its deal with Apple.

Now, evidence presented during that trial has become central to a class action against Apple in Canada, which a British Columbia Supreme Court judge recently certified.

The case was initially brought in 2021 by Spark Event Rentals Ltd., an event rental company based in British Columbia. The plaintiff alleged that Apple and Google conspired to limit competition in the search market, allowing Google to charge advertisers artificially inflated prices.

Apple, meanwhile, argued that its agreement with Google was a legitimate distribution arrangement rather than an unlawful conspiracy. The company also maintained that Google was the appropriate defendant, describing itself as an “innocent bystander.”

Interestingly, the lawsuit originally named both Apple and Google as defendants, but the plaintiff later dropped Google from the case following a dispute over an arbitration clause in its advertising contracts.

With Apple now the sole defendant, Justice Thomas has allowed the case to proceed as a class action, finding sufficient grounds to examine whether Google’s payments discouraged Apple from developing its own search engine.

The lawsuit seeks financial compensation for advertisers who allegedly overpaid for Google search ads, and the court has also allowed the question of punitive damages to proceed.

The class action covers Canadian residents who purchased search ads from Google since 2005, when Apple and Google first agreed to make Google the default search engine on Safari in exchange for a share of advertising revenue.

Importantly, the ruling does not establish that Apple engaged in anticompetitive conduct, but simply allows the allegations to proceed as a class action.

The central proposition raised by these pleadings is that Apple could have used its resources and distribution network to enter the search engine market, but chose not to because Google paid Apple billions of dollars in revenue-share payments to make Google the default search provider on Apple products. This arrangement gave Google market power, enabling it to charge supracompetitive advertising prices on search engines.

In my view, this pleads a common purpose to perform an act prohibited by s 45 of the Competition Act, such that it is not “clear and obvious” that the plaintiff has not pleaded an agreement between Google and Apple not to compete in the search engine market.

At one point in his decision, Justice Thomas cites Giannandrea’s testimony and directly quotes Cue’s from the US antitrust trial, before concluding that “this provides some basis in fact, supporting the inference that Apple did not compete with Google in the search engine market because of its Agreement with Google.”

Interestingly, the judge also acknowledges Apple’s objections to the evidence, agreeing that “the plaintiff has cherry-picked evidence to support his case,” but adding that, in his view, “it is appropriate to do so at this stage in the proceedings.”

With the class action greenlit, the case can now move forward toward trial, though no date has been announced yet.

#3398. 10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3396. 8 Years Later, Netflix’s Near-Perfect Political Thriller Is Still One of the Best Ever Made

Giovana Gelhoren is a High-Trending Topics Writer at Collider, covering the most-talked-about stars, movies, and TV shows. Before joining Collider, she was a Digital News Writer at People Magazine and served as Associate Editor at SheKnows, where she honed her expertise in celebrity coverage and entertainment journalism.

A proud Latina from Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, Giovana graduated from Northwestern University with a degree in Journalism and International Studies. She has interviewed countless celebrities, including Anne Hathaway, Halle Berry, Pamela Anderson, Jamie Lee Curtis, and Brenda Song, and is known for her encyclopedic knowledge of film, TV, and pop culture.

From Hostage to The Diplomat, Netflix has slowly but surely established itself as the go-to platform for well-done and fast-paced political thrillers. The Diplomat, for instance, hit the jackpot for the streaming giant, reaching not only unprecedented views as it gets renewed for a fifth season, but critical acclaim too, including 10 Primetime Emmy nominations and one recent win for Allison Janney in 2026 for Outstanding Supporting Actress in a Drama Series.

But while The Diplomat continues to dominate on Netflix, another 2018 political thriller on the platform is beginning to emerge as the perfect next watch for its viewers. The series Bodyguard, which first released on August 26, 2018, stars Richard Madden in his best role to date, and delivers a twisted, unpredictable tale involving political threats, international politics, and unbelievably high stakes.

Created by Jed Mercurio, Bodyguard follows war veteran and metropolitan police officer David Budd (Madden), as he earns a position as part of Protection Command after helping to diffuse a potential terrorist attack in the first fifteen minutes of the series. In the new role, David, who is currently separated from his wife Vicky (Sophie Rundle), and is struggling to connect with his two kids, is assigned to guard Julia Montague (Keeley Hawes), the UK's ambitious, polarizing Conservative Home Secretary. The catch: he fundamentally disagrees with everything she stands for. David, who suffers from PTSD from his time in combat, vehemently opposes her political agenda, including sending troops (himself included) to Afghanistan, and can't help but to be angered and question Julia's beliefs and policies.

From their first conversation, the tension is felt between the protagonists. David objects to everything Julia is fighting for, and she couldn't care less about his opinion. Nevertheless, she needs his reassurance that she will be protected at all times. While their dynamic is intriguing by itself, the plot soon thickens as David’s protection of Julia is fraught with attempts on her life, almost all of which he has some personal connection to. Soon, David finds himself in the middle of an intricate web of conspiracies connected to either himself or Julia. There's a political power play involving her sweeping new surveillance legislation, which earns her plenty of dangerous enemies in high places. There are people within her own political orbit who want her humiliated. There are people further out who want her dead. And there's at least one person in Budd's immediate circle whose loyalties are not what they appear to be. As he uncovers each of these puzzles pieces, the task of protecting Julia only becomes more and more challenging.

From the premise alone, it's safe to say Bodyguard is a Netflix must-watch. With complex opposing characters at its center, and a web of conspiracies that becomes all the more encompassing and dangerous as David investigates, the series has all the ingredients to be a gripping political thriller. On Rotten Tomatoes, the series was a hit, both with critics and audiences. The series earned 93% with critics, and 84% with audiences. "One of those rare shows that will have you hooked on the screen from the very first scene to the last," wrote one critic's review.

You said you’d watch one episode. That was eight hours ago.

Of course, another highlight is Madden himself, who first rose to fame in roles like Game of Thrones and Cinderella, and is showing a new side of himself in the six-episode series. "There are innumerable twists and turns to what becomes a kind of Whodunnit, but through it all, Madden makes us feel every single moment of what David is experiencing, most especially when confronting his insecurities about his failures as a husband and father," wrote Allison Keene in her review for Collider in 2018. "He has a job to do — several, in fact — and focusing on that is the only thing he believes is keeping him sane."

#3394. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

Meta has now launched Instagram Effect Builder to create AI imagery for use in Instagram Stories. While it’s a standalone web-based tool, the company is describing it as an expansion of the Edits app.

One quirk is that any effect you create becomes available to any Instagram user. This usage will, however, link back to your profile.

Today, we’re expanding what you can create with Edits and introducing a new way to share your creativity on Instagram […] With Effect Builder, you don’t need design or coding skills, or prior experience making effects. Describe the look you want, preview it on your own photos, and publish. The effect shows up in Instagram Stories for anyone to use, and whenever someone uses your effect we’ll link back to your profile so that it’s easy for others to find your work.

The web app is currently limited to adult Instagram users in the US.
