#3391. I tested the DJI Osmo 360 II and Insta360 needs to be seriously scared

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The DJI Osmo 360 II is the first (and, as I write this, the only) 360 camera to shoot 8K at 60fps. This makes it my top choice for high-octane 360 footage like motovlogging or extreme sports. Unlike its predecessor, the 360 II has user-replaceable lenses, and while battery life isn’t mind-blowing, it’s good enough at 8K/60fps. The only things I don’t like about the Osmo 360 II are its sky-high U.S. price and the internal audio wind reduction, which isn’t anything to write home about.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

“Uh oh,” is what Insta360 will doubtless have thought when the DJI Osmo 360 II launched. And it should’ve been worried. Up to now, Insta360 has been the undisputed king of 360 tech. But that reign has come to an end.

It all comes down to one thing: 8K/60fps, which the DJI Osmo 360 II can shoot. The flagship Insta360 X6, meanwhile, cannot, topping out at 8K/50fps. Insta360 is simply not there yet with the tech, and in fairness, that’s understandable. 8K at 60fps in 360 degrees puts extreme demands on a pocket-sized camera, its processor, memory, battery and thermals.

But somehow DJI has achieved it – which means it’s now ahead in the race. Even if the Osmo 360 II isn’t the best 360 camera in every area, it does the most important thing right now. It gives content creators the flexibility of 4K reframing from 360 footage at a frame rate fast enough for high-octane footage, and usable enough for YouTube.

So should you buy this camera? Find out in my full DJI Osmo 360 II review.

Unsurprisingly, given this is a flagship 360 camera, the Osmo 360 II isn’t cheap, opening the register at a whopping $699 in the U.S. at Amazon for the standard bundle with basic accessories. If you want accessories, the Adventure Combo I tested, with extra batteries and a selfie stick, costs $829. Of course, this is thanks to U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods. It’s also worth noting that, resulting from its feud with the U.S. government, DJI has withdrawn first-party support in the States, meaning no care plans if the camera needs repair.

In the U.K., the Osmo 360 II starts at £509, which undercuts the Insta360 X6 by over £100. And U.K. consumers also get access to a wider range of accessories bundles at Amazon, so they can tailor their spend to exactly what they need.

This pricing is comparable to the Insta360 X6, which also starts at $699. In my opinion, the 360 II is a much better buy thanks to the higher 60fps frame rate. In the U.K., where the 360 II is both more powerful and cheaper, it’s a total no-brainer. If you’re on a tighter budget, though, I’d advise checking out the Insta360 X5 ($549), GoPro MAX2 ($499) or the OG DJI Osmo 360 ($494). All shoot 8K 360 footage, just not at 60fps.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Osmo 360 II is designed more or less the same as its predecessor. It looks the same, measures the same, and weighs the same. That means it’s a squat-looking thing, especially compared to the lankier X6. It isn’t small though, at 2.4 x 1.4 x 3.2 inches, nor is it light at 6.4 ounces, so if you’re after something more suited to mounting on a helmet, check out an action camera like the DJI Osmo Action 6.

Versus the OG Osmo 360, there have been no radical updates to the display, which still isn’t an OLED; no updates to the internal memory, which is still 105GB (although over double the X6’s 47GB); and no updates to waterproofing, which is rated at 33 feet (half the 66 feet of the X6).

The controls are essentially the same, with two buttons on the back for recording and mode changing, a power button, and most tweaks done via the menu system or app. I found the Osmo 360 II’s record button fiddly to press with gloves on. And while I like DJI’s menu, it’s a little busy-feeling on the small display — the X6’s bigger display makes it slightly easier to use in the heat of the moment. Overall though, no major complaints controls-wise.

The Osmo 360 II uses the same quick-release mounting system as the previous gen, plus other DJI cameras like the Osmo Action 5 Pro, Action 6 and Osmo Nano. However, DJI has made a welcome quality-of-life update: the mount is now bi-directional. Previously, you had to get the mount the correct way round, which was annoying, but now it doesn’t matter. It may not sound like a big deal, but it’s kinda like going from USB-A to USB-C and makes the camera a lot quicker and easier to mount-unmount during shooting.

Again, the Osmo 360 II has no major updates to connectivity, with wireless data transfer, USB-C transfer and charging, and 105GB of internal memory, which should get you around 90 minutes of 8K footage — fantastic when you fill or forget a card. There’s Bluetooth and 2.4G for pairing to your phone, but DJI has added NFC connectivity which means you can pair the Osmo 360 II to your phone instantly just by placing the two together.

Where there has been a substantive update is lenses. The original Osmo 360 had non-replaceable lenses, which was a major drawback given all the competition had replaceable ones. 360 lenses are very easy to damage (in fact, my OG 360 was hit by a rock from a semi truck during testing, and DJI had to supply me with a replacement), so replaceable lenses are a huge deal.

The Osmo 360 had to be sent back to DJI for repair, which would be fine if you purchased a DJI care plan… only, you couldn’t buy one of those in the U.S. due to DJI’s ongoing feud with the federal government.

Thankfully, the simple solution has been employed, and the Osmo 360 II has replaceable lenses. Annoyingly, you can’t find official DJI replacement kits on Amazon (another repercussion of that feud with the government). In the U.K., this isn’t an issue, and an official DJI lens replacement kit will cost you just £22 at Amazon.

As always these days, DJI’s stabilization is pretty darn good. In most reframed 360 footage, you’ll be cropping a full 360 view down quite a bit, giving ample headroom for software stabilization (which is applied automatically by the app/desktop app in post production). I noticed a few jitters in wider fields of view, but nothing major.

In single-lens mode, the camera uses DJI’s usual RockSteady in-camera stabilization, and it works a treat. As you can see in the single-lens footage below, everything is beautifully smooth.

The Osmo 360 II’s headline feature is the most important: 8K/60fps. When recording high-octane footage, which is what 360 cameras are commonly used for, 60fps is a fast enough frame rate for smooth-looking footage. Fast-paced footage looks great at 60fps, with no choppiness whatsoever.

The original Osmo 360 and Insta360 X6 could only shoot at up to 50fps, which they might as well not do. 50fps is better than 30fps at smoothing out fast-moving footage, but is only really applicable to European television operating at 50Hz. The standards for online content, like YouTube, are 60fps for high octane and 30fps for everything else.

Thanks to 8K 360 footage, there’s also enough resolution headroom to reframe to 16:9 and maintain 4K when exporting. This all means that the Osmo 360 II is the first (and, as I write, only) 360 camera to let you shoot high-octane footage at high resolution and at a high frame rate.

The dual sensors in the 360 II are the same 1/1.1-Inch Square CMOS sensors as the OG 360. Frame rate is mainly decided by a camera’s image processing capabilities, and so that’s where the improvements have been made.

Unsurprisingly, given DJI is no newcomer to all this, footage looks excellent. The lenses are sharp, while colors look vivid but natural — more natural than Insta360’s typically saturated look.

Obviously, as a 360 camera, the primary benefit is ultimate framing flexibility. Shoot first, choose your fields of view and camera angles later. Aside from the selfie stick dead spot under the camera (which always shows on 360 cameras), stitching wasn’t noticeable, even at ultra-wide FoVs or in 360 modes like ‘Tiny Planet’, which is great.

With the new processing comes 14.5 stops of dynamic range. As such, the Osmo 360 II handles radical shifts in lighting very well, maintaining shadow detail and decreasing the frequency of blown-out highlights. This also benefits low-light performance, with the Osmo 360 II proving a substantial step up over its predecessor. in the equivalent SuperNight mode on both cameras at 8K/30p, the Osmo 360 II's footage looks brighter, sharper and less noisy than the OG Osmo 360. A solid upgrade, helped by the new processors.

Like most 360 cameras, you can also shoot in single-lens mode at up to 4K/120fps, using the Osmo 360 II like a traditional action cam. There’s a new mode called ‘Boost’ video which supposedly offers better quality than the normal video mode.

I asked DJI about this, but it was fairly tight-lipped on the technical explanation, telling me the mode simply widens the field of view to use more of the sensor — presumably the camera then oversamples the 4K output for a sharper image. As the whole (or most of) the sensor is being used, stabilization is affected, so standard video mode is better for shakier scenarios.

The Osmo 360 II packs some useful features for professional users or hardcore creators, including 10-bit color for extra flexibility when editing, and D-Log M for wider dynamic range capture when footage is going to be graded in post later.

The Osmo 360 II introduces a wind-shielded mic, helping to physically reduce wind buffeting alongside the in-camera wind reduction software algorithms. Overall, wind reduction is fine. There are three modes: ‘Standard’, ‘High’ and ‘Smart’ (which automatically adjusts between the first two). If you’re shooting in particularly windy conditions, like motorcycling, ‘High’ works well to reduce wind noise, although the microphones didn’t handle the loud noise of an engine particularly well, with some clipping — you can dial in some minus gain to help with this.

I wouldn’t say the Osmo 360 II’s internal audio is much better or worse than the X6, although both lose out to the Insta360 X5 — despite being a generation old now, the X5 still packs the best internal audio of any 360 camera I’ve tested.

Naturally, as a DJI product, the Osmo 360 II can hook up wirelessly over OsmoAudio to wireless DJI mics, like the DJI Mic 3 or DJI Mic Mini 2S. As they share an ecosystem, you get lots of control over the mics in-camera — control you wouldn’t get by simply connecting over Bluetooth. OsmoAudio is essentially Bluetooth, so audio quality in high dynamic range environments (like motorcycling) isn’t fantastic, but is more than enough for quieter scenarios and vlogging.

The DJI Mimo smartphone app is fairly solid these days. A few years back it was rather basic, but DJI has made strides to compete with Insta360’s app and the GoPro Quik app. There’s not much between them now, although Insta360’s app remains the easiest and most intuitive to use, especially for a straight-to-social workflow.

Mimo gives you a wide range of editing features, effects and export settings. It lets you do the basics, but I find reframing via keyframes a lot more clunky on Mimo versus the Insta360 app. Mimo feels more like a tool for whipping together quick client previews, assuming you’ll finesse footage later on a desktop. The Insta360 app makes it easier to put out smooth, polished content directly from your phone.

DJI has a big advantage for pros and serious creators, though. Both Insta360 and DJI offer desktop editing apps for more serious editing. However, pros will need their camera to fit in with existing workflows, and while both brands offer Premiere Pro 360 plug-ins, only DJI has them for DaVinci Resolve.

The Osmo 360 II’s battery life is a mixed bag. It features a bigger battery than the original Osmo 360, boosted from 1,950mAh to 2,150mAh. Despite this, in my standardized indoor tests, the Osmo 360 II only managed 88 minutes at 8K/30fps versus 112 minutes on the original model. Both pale in comparison to the 2,600mAh Insta360 X6, which managed 117 minutes at 8K/30fps.

That said, the OG model dropped off a cliff at higher frame rates. At 8K/50fps, the original camera only managed 30 minutes in my testing. The Osmo 360 II ran for 66 minutes at 8K/60fps and while it overheated after 45 minutes, it disabled its screen and ran for a further 21 minutes until dying. You’ll get longer while on the move, as wind chill will mean less thermal throttling. Still, 8K/60fps is no easy task, so 66 minutes is impressive.

At 8K/50fps, the Osmo 360 managed 77 minutes and overheated after around 50 (but again soldiered on, thermally throttled, for another 25 minutes. The X6 managed 90 minutes at 8K/50fps, but overheated every 20 minutes.

At 4K/60fps in single-lens mode, the Osmo 360 managed just over 80 minutes. Again, in the indoor stress test conditions, it overheated and thermally throttled itself after around 50 minutes, but kept on shooting for another half an hour before dying. Windchill will solve this. The X6, meanwhile, overheated at 33 minutes and only managed 56 minutes in total at 4K/60fps. Like I said, the Osmo 360 II’s battery life is a mixed bag, but where it counts at 60fps, it’s impressive.

Oof. When I reviewed the original Osmo 360, my sentiment was: “It’s a good start, but needs work.” Well, DJI has done the work, and a lot of it. The Osmo 360 II is the first 360 camera to reach 8K/60fps, making it ideal for creators who want the benefits of 360 recording without sacrificing frame rate.

The Osmo 360 II isn’t perfect, and whether you need this or the Insta360 X6 will, to a large extent, depend on what you’re doing or shooting. If your priority is a straight-to-social workflow, Insta360 still has the edge.

However, the margins between the two are mostly minor, all except one: frame rate. If you shoot high-octane footage — motovlogging, snowboarding, skydiving, etc. — there’s now only one camera to recommend. It has to be the Osmo 360 II.

#3390. Google DeepMind analysis proves Signal and WhatsApp encryption is secure

The Signal protocol has long been considered the gold standard for end-to-end encrypted messaging, with Edward Snowden a notable advocate. Now a Google DeepMind analysis has “formally verified” the security of the protocol.

In addition to its use in the Signal app, the same protocol is also used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, and the work has been described as “a landmark development” …

“Formal verification” is the term given to mathematically proving or disproving that a cryptographic algorithm or protocol satisfies its security claims under all conditions. It guarantees that there is no situation in which the protocol will fail. This is a far higher standard than traditional testing methods which seek to find vulnerabilities but cannot promise that others do not exist.

Using agentic AI to carry out formal verification is a huge breakthrough for cryptography and AI alike. It is, however, extremely computationally demanding, so Google told Wired it’s unclear as yet how practical it will be to use it more broadly.

DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process. “We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

It’s important to note that the validation is for the protocol itself rather than the Signal app as a whole. However, encouragement can be taken from the fact that when tested against older versions of Signal that contained known vulnerabilities, it identified those and flagged them as failing formal verification.

Also worth stating is that Google was able to build on some past formal verification work already completed without the use of AI. This analysis took four weeks, and the scale of resources required has not yet been disclosed, so we shouldn’t expect a whole array of other protocols to be validated overnight. All the same, this is a very big deal.

#3389. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

#3387. Guillermo del Toro’s Near-Perfect Fantasy Masterpiece Officially Returns in 1 Month

Guillermo del Toro is undeniably one of the most renowned horror directors of our time. While slashers, jump scares, and evil monsters (human or otherwise) rule the genre and are often fan-favorite tropes, del Toro brings a unique blend of gothic horror, dark fantasy, and fairy tales to his work, presenting them through a sympathetic, artistic lens. Features like the Jacob Elordi-led Frankenstein, Cronos, Crimson Peak, and more give audiences a unique look at monsters, who are usually the genre's antagonists.

Among such notable titles from del Toro is Pan’s Labyrinth, which seamlessly blends ruthless historical drama with a child’s imaginative fairytale. Set in post-Civil War fascist Spain, ten-year-old Ofelia moves with her pregnant mother to a remote mountain outpost run by her cruel stepfather, Captain Vidal. While Vidal ruthlessly hunts anti-fascist rebels, Ofelia discovers an ancient labyrinth and meets a mysterious Faun. Things take a turn when the Faun reveals she is the reincarnation of an underworld princess and assigns three perilous tasks to prove her immortality before the full moon. Navigating both fairy-tale monsters and wartime brutality, Ofelia succeeds until her final test demands her newborn brother’s blood.

The film explores themes of choice and disobedience through Ofelia’s character arc. Further, the narrative contrasts the brutality of totalitarianism with childhood imagination. As with every del Toro movie, life, death, and rebirth drive the narrative, unfolding each moment with equal wonder and horror. The feature won three Academy Awards that season and earned a 95% Rotten Tomatoes score from critics.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

#3383. Ring’s wheeled and flying robots will patrol your home

Some people use a whole bunch of fixed cameras to monitor their homes, but Amazon has just announced a more flexible solution through wheeled and flying robots.

Both the $250 Drone Cam and $1,000 Rover Cam can respond to alarms or door and window sensor alerts in order to go check out what’s happening and send live video …

Amazon says they are the first two Ring Robotics products, with more likely to follow. Both are autonomous.

Ring Drone and Ring Rover are both powered by AI Pilot, a custom-built system that uses the devices’ cameras, specialized vision models, on-device sensors, and cloud processing to see, think, and navigate autonomously.

AI Pilot simplifies the customer experience, starting with setup. Simply carry Ring Drone through your space or let Ring Rover autonomously explore, and it turns what it sees into a floor plan. It intelligently identifies rooms and suggests patrol points: spots worth extra attention. This could be a side door, windows, a register, or a long corridor, helping eliminate guesswork while also allowing you to add additional points customized to your space and security preferences.

When a patrol or flight is initiated, AI Pilot plans the most efficient route to get to a preset point based on the map it’s created. From there, it reacts in real time—autonomously navigating around furniture, shelving, and any obstacle it encounters.

You can set either device to patrol on a fixed schedule, as well as activate them manually, but they will also automatically respond to sensor alerts and alarms.

When a Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, [either device] automatically [moves] to previously set patrol points to investigate […] Continuous person motion detection means Ring Rover can alert you and start recording the moment it detects motion in its view—even when docked.

The Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping on December 16 for $999.99, but you can preorder it today. The Drone Cam starts shipping in late January for $249.99, but there’s no preorder yet.

#3381. Adobe unveils new AI tools for Photoshop, Premiere, and more, with MCP support coming in 2027

Adobe today announced a sweeping set of updates at its annual Adobe MAX conference, focused on giving users more ways to automate complex workflows, edit content, and work across its creative apps. Here are the details.

At the Adobe MAX event today, the company unveiled a series of features, many of them AI-powered or AI-assisted, that will begin rolling out across its suite of creative platforms as early as today.

In Photoshop, the new Relight tool offers a way to non-destructively and dynamically add, reposition, and resize light sources in the composition, while Generative Restylelets users** prompt the platform to generate variations of an image’s style and fine-tune the results using adjustable sliders.

Photoshop is also adding a Quick Compare slider to make it easier to track before-and-after results, and is getting several features in the beta app, including, per Adobe:

Following its acquisition of Topaz Labs, Adobe is also introducing two new AI image enhancement models: Wonder 4, which combines upscaling, denoising, deblurring, and sharpening into a single operation, and Image HDR, which converts standard images into HDR with improved brightness and detail.

Adobe Premiere is also getting generative tools that make it easier to prepare raw files for a project, including Enhance Audio, Separate Crosstalk, and Separate Sound Source. Adobe is also adding a Generative Remove tool to Premiere in beta, “bringing you the power to remove unwanted objects, like boom mics and logos or background distractions, directly on your timeline,” says the company.

Premiere is also getting Color Mode, a new color-grading tool starting today, which “supports everything from quick corrections to more advanced grades while keeping your video as the focus.”

Another interesting tool making its way into Premiere is Generative Media Tool. Here’s Adobe:

The Generative Media Tool brings Generate Video, Generate Sound Effects, Generate Soundscape and Generate Music directly into your timeline in Premiere. You can generate missing b-roll, background music or sound for a scene using context from your edit, then keep refining the result in your timeline. You can also choose from Adobe Firefly and models from partners including Google, Kling, Runway and Luma based on the creative needs of your project.

As for iPhone users who rely on Premiere Mobile, Adobe announced that its newly established partnerships with UMG and WMG will bring hundreds of thousands of licensed music tracks to the app (for non-commercial use) starting today, with users able to explore trending songs, discover featured artists, and create videos using artist-inspired templates.

Premiere mobile is also getting agentic tools soon, including Quick Cuts, which generates a first cut based on the user’s prompt and the materials they add, and an AI Assistant, which helps users find the right editing tools and execute tasks based on natural language instructions.

In Lightroom, the company is adding multiple new tools that make it easier to edit or more quickly fix small imperfections. That includes Glow, which “adds soft, cinematic light to your photos,” Blemish Removal for quick skin fine-tuning, Open Eyes in beta, and an improved and expanded Camera Tethering on Desktop and the iPad, with support for more cameras and advanced shooting controls, plus the ability to connect cameras directly to an iPad for live previews and photo editing.

Adobe is adding new brushes, gradients, patterns, and graphic styles to Illustrator, alongside new Blend controls, which “make it easier to develop and refine designs with a persistent control panel and live preview,” per the company.

As for InDesign, a new Co-editing feature, available in beta, streamlines collaborative work, while the new Flex Layout tool dynamically adjusts content based on the canvas size and artwork. InDesign is also getting Check Document and Rewrite that more quickly “help identify common editorial and accessibility issues while you’re still working.”

While it will not launch until 2027, this feature will enable users to connect Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, and After Effects to the AI tools and agents they already use.

In practice, this will mean connecting Photoshop to ChatGPT and having them work in tandem to adapt an entire campaign based on new artwork you develop and attach to your prompt.

This integration will also account for other connected tools, so the user can ask ChatGPT to make edits, add new files to a Google Drive folder, update the team on Slack, and so on.

Here’s Adobe on the upcoming MCP integration:

Because it runs locally on your computer, your agent works directly in your native project files, and your layers, vectors, bins and sequences stay editable.

The company notes that MCP integrations will enter private beta in early 2027, and users can sign up here to learn more.

According to Adobe, Firefly is getting even better at helping users organize and edit their raw material for tasks such as turning travel clips into a vlog, creating social media campaigns, or assembling videos from storyboards.

The new Firefly Video lets users organize scenes, assemble clips, add captions, and generate transitions and B-roll, while Firefly Design brings illustration, image editing, animation, and 3D tools into a single canvas.

Adobe is also adding Quick Actions for common editing tasks, Firefly Graph for creating reusable workflows, and Firefly Builder (in private beta) for prototyping websites and apps using natural language.

Firefly’s AI Assistant is also getting new capabilities, including Plan Mode, which lets users review and approve an agent’s proposed actions, and Model Selector, which lets them choose which AI model to use.

Adobe is also previewing Always-on agents, which can handle recurring tasks such as organizing assets, checking quality, and preparing content for different platforms in the background, even when users step away.

Adobe is also expanding its Creative Agent across Creative Cloud, with AI Assistants now available in beta in Illustrator, Premiere, InDesign, After Effects, and Frame.io, as well as the Photoshop beta app.

These assistants allow users to execute complex, multi-step tasks using natural language prompts. In Premiere, for example, users can ask the assistant to apply effects to an entire sequence, track subjects across frames, or adjust color and exposure across multiple clips.

To learn more about these and other features announced at Adobe MAX today, stay tuned to the company’s blog.

#3377. The 10 Best Fire-Type Pokemon, Ranked

From being one of the three different types from a trainer's first starter Pokémon to powerful legendaries that create scorching infernos, Fire-type Pokémon have been a staple of the franchise from the very beginning. While there aren't as many Fire-types compared to the other two starter types, the 103 different Pokémon that feature the Fire type are so rich with charm and blazing power that it's no surprise that the type has been an absolute fan-favorite.

When at their best, Fire-types can feature some of the most exceptional offensive of any Pokémon type, quite literally being unmatched in terms of their firepower with attacks that eviscerate opponents. Combined with the strengths of being more powerful in the Sun and the burn status effect, there are many different ways for a Fire-type to find great success with distinguished strengths throughout Pokémon history. While everyone is going to have their own personal pick for their favorite Fire type, these 10 consistently stand out as some of the best Pokémon that the type has to offer.

One of the three mythical Pokémon from Generation V and one of Pokémon's best balances of overwhelming cute factor with destructive power, Victini has been an icon ever since its debut in Pokémon Black and White. The Victory Pokémon is said to guarantee victory for any trainer who uses it, and even if this isn't the case in terms of gameplay, its overwhelming strengths certainly make the path to victory an easy one for trainers who utilize it.

It's Psychic/Fire type gives it incredible offensive potential, made even more powerful with its powerful exclusive moves, Searing Shot and V-create. Not only does it hit incredibly hard, but with its base 600 stat total, with 100 in each stat, makes it an excellent all-rounder in terms of defense and speed, able to adapt to any type of opponent. The only thing that has held it back is that, by virtue of being a mythical Pokémon, there are very few official ways to receive this powerful and adorable Pokémon.

One of the three legendary birds that make up the very first legendary trio in the series, Moltres was the original go-to choice for a powerful Fire-type Pokémon, with its design largely paralleling and finding inspiration from the iconic phoenix. Even after 30 years of power-creep and additional Fire-types that have taken its mantle, the Pokémon continues to find strength in the modern day, largely utilizing its exceptional defensive ability Flame Body and its highly versatile move pool.

The Pokemon has frequently made appearances throughout the series as a Legendary able to be caught, even outside of its home region of Kanto. It's about as consistently strong as a Fire-type can get, although it got considerably more viable as an option after the addition of the Heavy-Duty Boots item, which stopped it from losing half its health to Stealth Rocks. Moltres even received an exciting new Galarian Form in Pokemon Sword and Shield, complete with the exclusive move Fiery Wrath, but this alternate form sadly isn't a Fire-type.

For a long time in the Pokémon series, the Bug-type was associated with weak, low-power Pokémon that were useful in the early game, but never stayed as a permanent member of the team. One of the biggest Pokémon that helped change this perception was Volcarona, the Bug/Fire-type that, while taking a long time and lots of investment to evolve, is one of the strongest non-Legendary Pokémon of all time. Its level of power is so high that some people are often mistaken and believe it to be a Legendary.

Volcarona's exceptional strength comes from its usage of good speed, high attacking power, and usage of one of the greatest setup moves of all time, Quiver Dance, which makes its already great strengths even better. It also features an incredibly striking and beautiful design, being a beautiful moth creature with fires so powerful that it provided a replacement for the sun by ancient people.

The newest Fire-type legendary that was just recently introduced in Pokémon Scarlet and Violet, Chi-Yu has completely redefined the concept of a strong Fire-Type in the eyes of trainers. This specially offensive member of the treasures of ruin is defined by its powerful ability, Beads of Ruin, which lowers the special defense of everyone else on the field, making its already powerful fire attacks even more powerful. It proved to be so powerful that it became one of the only Pokemon to be directly nerfed in a patch, with its base Special Attack stat being lowered in the Day 1 patch for the game.

Still, with overwhelming power coming from its Overheats and Dark Pulses, Chi-Yu has some of the highest and most immediate damage potential out of any modern Pokémon. It seems a little silly that so much power can come from such a tiny fish, but Chi-Yu is a Pokémon that should not be underestimated, as it will wipe away opponents in a blaze of destructive flames.

Arguably the fan-favorite member of Generation II's iconic trio of legendary beasts that were resurrected after the burning of Brass Tower, Entei has been an icon of blazing power ever since its debut. Even from the early days, Entei was given considerably more attention than the other two members of its trio, most notably getting a prominent leading role in its own movie, Pokemon 3: The Movie. This singular appearance in one of the best Pokemon movies alone has made it a fan-favorite Fire-type, yet its consistent strengths over the years further amplify its icon status.

With high-power moves like Eruption, Sacred Fire, and Extreme Speed at its disposal, Entei is a powerhouse of offense while also having some of the best HP stats of any Fire-type. Entei even managed to get a considerable buff in later generations with its newer hidden ability Inner Focus, making it immune to flinching and incredibly useful in the official VGC format. Entei also directly correlates to its paradox relative, Gouging Fire, the Fire/Dragon type that is seen as an ancient relative of Entei from the far past.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Over 25% of all Fire-Type Pokémon are starters, so it simply makes sense that some of the most memorable and impactful Fire-Types just happen to be the ones that many trainers start off their journey with. This trend continues into the modern age of Pokémon with Cinderace, the soccer player rabbit who fires off burning soccer balls to deal devastating damage to opponents. It's exclusive moves Pyro Ball and Court Change, give it an immediate presence in a battle, not just with high power, but able to completely shift the tides of battle.

A major part of Cinderace being such a powerful starter is its usage of the ability Libero, which parallels the previous Protean ability and allows Cinderace to change its type by using a move, catching the opponent off guard and giving it exceptional offensive and defensive capabilities. It also features a memorable Gigantamax form, where it grows super long ears and balances on top of a giant flaming fireball.

The Fire/Steel legendary Pokémon from Generation IV that has utilized its power over magma and volcanic surroundings to deal powerful damage to opponents, Heatran may not be as immediately iconic as the other Gen IV legendaries, but deservedly earns a reputation as one of its strongest. With its signature move Magma Storm, Heatran deals out loads of damage, not just from the initial hit itself, but from residual damage each turn that keeps the opponent stuck on the field.

Heatran's only major weakness that it has to look out for is its 4x weakness to Ground-type moves, but a well-utilized Air Balloon item and some half-decent defenses can help a skilled trainer navigate its weakness while making its strengths all the more impactful. Heatran also has all sorts of eyes on its potential with its recent new mega evolution, with Mega Heatran making its debut in Pokemon Legends: Z-A, but will finally be able to use for traditional battles in Pokemon Champions in December.

The final evolution of the very first Fire-type starter and the mascot Pokémon for Pokémon Red, Charizard is synonymous with the Fire-type as a whole, for many being the unbreakable symbol for blazing glory in the series. Being one of the fan-favorites of the series, Charizard has received a lot of love in all different corners of the franchise. From being playable in Super Smash Bros. to extremely expensive Pokémon cards to standout appearances in the anime.

However, in terms of the core main series of games, Charizard's greatest strengths arise in the frequent new forms it has received over the years, including two mega evolutions in Mega Charizard Y and Mega Charizard X, as well as a Gigantamax form used by Pokémon Sword and Shield's champion, Leon. Mega Charizard Y especially being able to both set the sun and make exceptional use of its offensive potential makes it one of the strongest Mega Pokémon to date, completely dominating the meta of Pokemon Champions.

The mascot pokemon for Pokémon Gold and its remake Pokémon HeartHold, Ho-Oh's exceptional defenses combined with great offenses and overwhelming stats has continously made it one of the strongest Pokemon of all time. The rainbow bird is a symbol of glory and pure-hearted kindness in the Pokemon world, with its bright shining lights making it a beautiful sight to behold for the trainers who witness it. Ho-Oh also famously had its first appearance in the first episode of the Pokemon anime, with Ash witnessing it flying across the sky, as it was a complete mystery until the Generation II games were released.

In battles, Ho-Oh absolutely lives up to its mythos and popularity, having one of the highest base stat totals of any Fire-type Pokémon, one of the best abilities in the game in Regenerator, and one of only 2 Pokémon with access to Sacred Fire. Ho-Oh's role as a defensive Legendary that can still deal out massive damage has made it a consistent threat ever since its introduction, as well as a continuous fan-favorite all these years later.

While Blaziken may not be as overwhelmingly iconic and recognizable as Charizard in terms of Fire-type starter status, the Fire/Fighting type has arguably reached higher highs in terms of overwhelming strength in-game and an incredibly endearing design. The blazing chicken dedicated to fiery kicks was already a massive icon in its debut game, but everything changed for the Pokemon when it recieved its hidden ability, Speed Boost.

With the ability to increase its speed every turn, Blaziken soon turned into one of the greatest setup sweepers of all time, able to snowball into an unstoppable fiery force that completely destroyed teams. Even more egregiously strong was when Blaziken's star-power and fan-favorite status gave it a super-powerful Mega evolution, one that it received before its fellow Generation III starters and still maintained the Speed Boost ability. With some of the highest power and speed of any Pokémon, fire-type or otherwise, teams unprepared for Blaziken inevitably go up in flames.

#3373. Apple’s new HomeView to add two major features not yet announced, per leaks

Apple’s HomeView arrives this Friday (pre-order here), but leaks indicate there are already two major new features in the works that haven’t been announced. Here’s what to expect.

It’s been a busy product launch season for Apple, and the company isn’t done quite yet.

Two new Home products arrive in stores this Friday, November 13: Apple HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K.

Yet despite the HomeView still being days away from launch, leaks in Apple code have already revealed two unannounced features that are in the works.

Leaker pdfu discovered evidence in HomeView 27.2 software that Apple is preparing for the product to add security camera functionality.

Based on pdfu’s findings, much of the work has already been done for HomeView to integrate with HomeKit Secure Video.

However, Apple hasn’t announced any sort of security camera functionality, so there’s clearly still more work to be done and it’s always possible the feature is never enabled.

Additionally, pdfu found a key change in iOS 27.3’s beta that reveals support for third-party AI apps is coming to HomeView.

HomeView has a unique third-party app story. There’s no App Store, but the product can run CarPlay-compatible apps from your iPhone automatically. At launch, only audio and video apps will be supported.

But iOS 27.3’s beta code adds “conversational apps” as a third category of supported apps. That’s what AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude are classified as in CarPlay.

Nobody should buy a HomeView in the hope of these two features being added. But if you are interested in HomeView, it sounds like Apple has an ambitious set of software updates planned for its new product.

You can pre-order Apple’s HomeView here for $299.

Would either of these HomeView additions impact a purchase decision for you? Let us know in the comments.

#3371. Riverboat Cruise Capsizes After Oil Tanker Crash Near New Orleans, Video

1:57 PM PT -- CNN reports that dozens of patients have been admitted to a local hospital following the crash.

Cruise ship passengers ended up in the Mississippi River on Friday when an oil tanker hit the side of the ship and capsized it.

Video captured the wild scene, which took place near New Orleans ... and shows the tanker -- Atlantic Asphalt -- running directly into the side of American Heritage, the river cruise ship.

It's unclear why the tanker ran into the ship at this time ... but it hit the ship hard enough to flip it on its side -- and reports say multiple passengers were flung into the water, where they were later rescued.

The ship slowly sank while authorities rushed to the scene. The Port of New Orleans states that 150 people were aboard the cruise at the time of the accident.

American Heritage was docked at the Crescent City Connection bridge when Atlantic Asphalt ran into it.

It's unclear how many people -- if any -- were injured in the collision.

#3366. Apple TV launches new sign language accessibility feature

Apple today launched a neat new accessibility feature for the Apple TV streaming service. Users will now have the option to watch with a sign language interpretation for some of Apple’s original movies.

The feature is launching this Friday with the debut of the new film Being Heumann, as well as F1: The Movie. Support for more titles will follow later.

Alongside those two films, Apple said that sign language options will be available for Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid later this year, with more to come.

To access the new functionality, you need to be using the Apple TV app on iPhone, iPad or Mac running 27.2 or later. The feature will also be available on some versions of the Apple TV app on other platforms.

By default, the Sign Language controls are hidden. If you want to use the feature, firstly go to the Settings app -> TV app, and enable the Sign Language display.

Then, on eligible titles, a new Sign Language button will appear in the player controls. You can simply toggle to enable, and choose from American Sign Language or British Sign Language modes.

When enabled, a signing interpreter then appears in the corner of the frame, synced with the video playback.

When browsing the catalog, sign language availability will also be shown next to the usual subtitle and audio language information. Users will also be able to search “with ASL” or “with BSL” to find compatible titles.

You can see it with prolific authors, busy filmmakers, and then also with artists. If an artist or band hasn’t released anything bad as far as albums are concerned, then they're either a rare breed of artist/band, or they’ve not released a ton of albums.

These artists are all great, but each has put out at least one album of questionable quality, and said not-great albums are below. So, it’s a bit negative, critiquing those albums, but it’s also good to remember that an artist has to be pretty great to be included here, with the albums below standing out since they're generally surrounded by other compelling albums.

With a debut album in 1967 and a final release almost half a century later, it would've been truly surprising if David Bowie never misfired critically. As it stands, him only having a few misses is still remarkable, and then when you take into account just how high-quality most of his good albums were, it does make those less-than-great ones easier to forgive.

If you're not singling out his self-titled debut, you're probably going to turn to one of two 1980s albums by Bowie to mark as his weakest. At least 1984’s Tonight has “Loving the Alien,” while Never Let Me Down, which seemed like it was supposed to be a comeback after Tonight was largely critically dismissed, doesn’t really have any highlights. You're better off sticking with Scary Monsters (and Super Creeps) and Let's Dance if you want to hear some ‘80s Bowie, and then all his post-1980s stuff is more interesting than Never Let Me Down, too.

It feels a little hard to get too angry at Raditude, partly because it’s already been criticized to hell and back, and partly because that album cover is hilarious and it might feel nicer to pretend to be in on the joke. Because Raditude is almost definitely a joke. Also, it’s called “Raditude.” Weezer are a ridiculous band, but they do have ridiculous or somewhat eyebrow-raising albums that are of a higher quality than Raditude.

The opening track, “(If You're Wondering If I Want You To) I Want You To,” is kind of fun, but otherwise, you don’t have a lot here to really grab onto.

Even as far as funny album covers and titles go, Raditude can’t be the funniest combo, since Weezer also have an album named Hurley, and the cover is just a close-up of Jorge Garcia’s face (he played Hurley on Lost). How can you get too mad at a band that does that? It’s funny. That absurdity and willingness to be a meme can be appreciated, but if you're looking at Raditude specifically, and the music itself, uh, the opening track, “(If You're Wondering If I Want You To) I Want You To,” is kind of fun, but otherwise, you don’t have a lot here to really grab onto or remember.

While no one is going to mistake Weezer for Metallica, St. Anger does occupy a similar space critically to Raditude. All the bad things that could be said about an album have been said about these two, as notorious 2000s albums, yet with Metallica, it was a bit more of a downfall, since their heyday was in the 1980s, rather than the 1990s, like Weezer. Also, Weezer sort of bounced back in the 2010s, and the same can’t really be said about Metallica.

Sorry, it’s true. That doesn’t take away from that 1980s run, and then even in the 1990s, there was still some good stuff Metallica-wise. The good times can’t last forever, though. Eventually, there have to be sad times. Mad times. Angry times. St. Anger times. It gets worse for Metallica, though. Look a little further down, for another notorious album that came out eight years on from this one.

You can’t win here, because there will be people who don’t like the suggestion that Taylor Swift is a great artist, and there'll probably also be people who like everything she’s done and thereby won’t like The Life of a Showgirl being criticized. To the people in the first camp, she’s done some great stuff and is popular for good reason. To the people in the other camp, she is capable of so much more.

The Life of a Showgirl felt a little worse than being just Taylor Swift on autopilot. There are three somewhat solid songs at the start, and then the whole thing derails, with some truly questionable lyrics and a lot of repetition as far as the music itself goes (even for stuff belonging to the pop genre). It can only be up from here, for Swift. Well, at least it’s hard to imagine something missing the mark more than The Life of a Showgirl any time soon.

Calling a Michael Jackson album bad is about as risky as calling a Taylor Swift album bad, or maybe even a little more so, since he has dedicated fans as well, and saying Invincible (the album that ended up being his last) is bad probably constitutes a hot take. But Invincible is such a slog. It doesn’t have to be as good as Thriller, because not much is, but wow does that classic album move.

And it also feels coherent. There are other great Michael Jackson albums where you can also admire the consistency and flow. With his 1990s stuff, maybe a little less so, but at least there were more highlights. Invincible is trying to do too much and please too many people all at once, and the resulting album is one where you feel like you're fighting to stay focused throughout. The album should be focused, and you shouldn’t have to do all that work yourself. Invincible, honestly, is a chaotic mess of an album. Sorry.

There might be some more recent Kanye West albums that are worse than Jesus Is King, but this was his first real miss, rather than just putting out something divisive, and also, some of these recent albums just aren’t fun to engage with or even think about. You do have to acknowledge things have gotten worse on a quality front (2021’s Donda, though, was better than Jesus Is King), and also that Kanye West, as a figure, has continued escalating the questionable things he’s willing to do and say.

Knowledge of 2020s Kanye West makes Jesus Is King look even more absurd in hindsight. It was a weirdly clean-cut Christian hip-hop album that felt a bit rushed and bizarrely produced at the time, and now it just feels bizarre, clashing with the very unwholesome things West has returned to doing. It’s around this point where it really started feeling not worth keeping up, even if you'd weathered the storm(s) up until that point.

Since Lou Reed was credited alongside Metallica for Lulu, Metallica can sneak back on here for a second time, or more accurately, they're here 1.5 times. Lulu is more notorious than St. Anger, in any event, but neither Metallica nor Lou Reed were strangers to making divisive albums. The former had St. Anger, and the latter had Metal Machine Music, which is a wild one (research in your own time and at your own risk).

They collided to make Lulu, though, and the result was something people either gave up on long ago, or are still trying to make some kind of sense of a decade and a half later. If someone tells you they “get” Lulu, maybe they're geniuses. It’s possible. But if someone tells you they both get and genuinely enjoy Lulu, run away from them as fast as you possibly can.

The jokes write themselves. The Clash released an album called Cut the Crap and it was… yeah. It was the band’s final album and ended what had otherwise been a pretty great run on a real bummer, because the lead-up to making it and then the production was something that pushed the members of The Clash apart, and then its negative reception when it did finally see the light of day was a real nail in the coffin sort of thing.

Best to remember the good times. You know, London Calling, the self-titled album, maybe about half of Sandinista, and a fair few songs on Combat Rock, too. You can’t go too wrong with most of the other albums by The Clash, but you also can’t go right with anything on Cut the Crap. The legendary punk rock band was mortal/human after all.

There’s a great documentary called The Endless Summer. It isn't specifically related to The Beach Boys, but it did come out in 1966, when the band was at its peak (Pet Sounds!), and then The Endless Summer was about surfing, as were quite a few early songs by The Beach Boys. Anyway, if you wanted to argue there was some way to keep riding the high of the 1960s, continuing the summer with surfing and Beach Boys, maybe you could, at least until 1992.

Just over a quarter of a century on from all that optimism and literal sunshine came Summer in Paradise. Whether you even want to count it as a true Beach Boys album… definitely debatable. Brian Wilson wasn’t involved at all, and that’s otherwise unheard of for a Beach Boys album. And it’s been partially erased from history, in the sense that it’s out-of-print and hasn’t been reissued, and you can’t even find official uploads on the band’s channel on YouTube. They seem to want you to forget about it, and maybe you'll want to forget about it, too, should you be subjected to Summer in Paradise.

Hey, you’ve made it this far. And I’ve made it this far. Since we’ve made it this far, I’m going to get personal, and that’s where the “I’ve” and the “I’m” come in. And “I,” as in I really loved Arcade Fire. This band was everything for a while there, definitely before Everything Now, but even that album had its moments. The band’s first three albums were basically perfect. The follow-up to Everything Now, We, was a step in the right direction. And between the first three great albums and Everything Now, there was 2013’s Reflektor, which has always felt underappreciated and might well get the proper amount of love it deserves one day.

That’s all to say I either loved or felt okay with defending all of Arcade Fire’s first six albums. Then album #7 came out and I couldn’t finish it. Pink Elephant contained some of the dullest and most lifeless music I’d ever heard. I’ve listened to some albums by this band dozens, or possibly even hundreds, of times. I couldn’t get through the sonic sludge that was Pink Elephant a single time. What the actual hell happened here? Look how they massacred my boy…

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3363. iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta, and it introduces a new iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.

I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.

But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.

For example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.

I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a new optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if you have ‘Windowed Apps’ enabled you’ll see a new option below it: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom’

If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this new setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.

When the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.

I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The new setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.

Will you enable this new iPadOS 27.3 setting? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments.

#3362. Garmin Enduro 4 review: monster MIP battery life makes this a value alternative to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is an iterative update on the Garmin Enduro 3 but offers a compelling alternative to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro. It’s cheaper, lighter and offers more battery life than Garmin’s flagship, and it's one of the best adventure watches available.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Memory-in-pixel displays are becoming rarer on the best Garmin watches, but those who prefer them are still well served by the Enduro line. If battery life is your primary concern, the Enduro 4 delivers in spades.

It lasted me 16+ days on a charge, around 50% longer than even the best sports watches with AMOLED displays for battery life, like the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro or Suunto Vertical 2.

Garmin hasn’t held back on features either, with the Enduro 4 getting most of the same key sports tracking tools as the Fenix 9 Pro, in a lighter case and at a lower price.

It’s an attractive package, but the elephant in the room is that the Enduro 3 is also getting nearly all the same new features as the Enduro 4 through software updates, has a similar design and the same incredible battery life, and undercuts the new watch in sales.

The Garmin Enduro 4 launched in October 2026 and costs $899 in the U.S. and £799 in the U.K. It’s the same launch price in the U.S. as the Enduro 3, but the latter is now available for £699/$799.

It’s a cheaper alternative to the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro Solar, which is the MIP option of the Fenix line-up and starts at $1,099.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is a large but lightweight watch that uses Garmin’s familiar five-button setup. It has a 51mm case and is thick, but being mostly made from plastic means it’s significantly lighter than the 51mm watch in the Fenix 9 line-up.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It has a titanium bezel and a sapphire crystal screen with solar panels to boost the impressive battery life even further in sunny conditions.

The memory-in-pixel display is clear enough to read in all conditions, though I do think the Enduro 4 is less bright and readable than Garmin’s AMOLED watches when indoors or under tree cover.

There are some hardware changes and improvements from the Enduro 3. The Enduro 4 has a silver bezel with fewer yellow highlights, and under the hood it has more RAM, a faster processor for maps, and double the storage (64GB vs. 32GB on the Enduro 3).

The new watch also comes with Garmin’s new ComfortFit band, which I like a lot more than the UltraFit band that ships with the Enduro 3, though you can also buy the ComfortFit band separately.

On the top of the watch is a built-in flashlight with four brightness levels and a red mode, and on its underside is Garmin’s Elevate Gen 5 heart rate sensor, which is the same sensor as the Fenix 9 series and Enduro 3.

While it’s not a diveproof watch like the Fenix 9, the Enduro 4 has a 10 ATM rating and is waterproof. It also lacks the mic and speaker you do get on the Fenix.

Despite its size, I found the Enduro 4 comfortable to wear 24/7 throughout testing. It’s not as attractive as the all-titanium Fenix 9 Pro, but the Enduro 4 is still a good-looking watch to wear outside your training.

Unless you’re desperate to go diving, the Enduro 4 has all the customizable sports modes you could ever need to track your workouts, including the improved rucking and rowing modes introduced on the Fenix 9.

Runners, cyclists, swimmers and triathletes get the most detail in their sports modes, including an improved stamina feature that aims to provide guidance on how much energy you have left in endurance activities and how best to pace them.

The Enduro 4 feeds all the data you track during workouts into an extensive suite of training analysis tools.

It has all the top-of-the-range features you get on the Garmin Forerunner 970 and Fenix 9, including running economy estimates (when paired with the Garmin HRM 600 chest strap) and ratings for overall endurance and hill-running ability.

Garmin offers greater depth of training analysis than any other brand I’ve tested, and while you might not want or need all this data, it’s there if you do, while a simple stat like overall training readiness provides a one-stop shop for those who want info at a glance.

I tested the GPS accuracy of the Enduro 4 by looking at its tracks after runs and comparing them with other watches that have proved reliably accurate on this front over time, like the Fenix 9 Pro and Coros Pace 4 Pro.

Garmin’s multi-band GPS accuracy is as good as it gets in my experience, and the Enduro 4 was reliably excellent throughout my testing, with consistent pacing and accurate GPS tracks when running in suburbs, city centers and under tree cover.

The heart rate accuracy was also good. I compared the Enduro 4’s readings with a chest strap in each workout, and it almost always closely aligned with the strap.

During interval workouts, the Enduro 4’s optical heart rate sensor would lag a little behind the chest strap, and I did spot the occasional error at the start of runs on cold days, but I’d say the overall accuracy was very good. If you want more reliable results, I’d say you’d need a chest strap.

Battery life is a key selling point of the Enduro 4, and it didn't disappoint on this front in my testing.

The listed stats have the watch lasting 30 days in watch mode, or up to 90 days in sufficiently sunny conditions, and offering 60 hours of GPS in its most accurate mode (90 hours with solar).

If you use battery saver mode, the watch can last indefinitely in sunny conditions, and if you slum it and use regular GPS tracking (which is still pretty accurate), you can track activities for 120 hours (320 hours with solar).

On my first charge, the watch lasted me 16 days, and it’s tracking to go longer on my second charge; numbers that outperform the longest-lasting AMOLED watches comfortably, and the Enduro 4 also offers better battery life than the MIP Fenix 9 Pro Solar.

The only watches that rival the Enduro 4’s battery life are other MIP options like the Garmin Instinct 3 Solar, Coros Vertix 2S and the Enduro 3, which matches the newer watch on this front.

It’s also worth noting I was testing the Enduro 4 in cloudy conditions almost all the time, and got barely any extra juice out of the solar panels, so if you live in a sunnier climate and spend a lot of time outdoors, you can expect even better battery life.

Many of the exclusive updates on the Enduro 4 compared with the Enduro 3 relate to its mapping features. On the hardware side, you have a faster processor and more RAM, so maps should load more quickly when zooming and panning.

Then, when using the maps, you can use a new perspective view, which I prefer to the top-down view of your location on the Enduro 3, though it’s hardly a life-changing update.

The speed boost is welcome, and it’s noticeable when panning around maps on the watches side-by-side, but again, this wasn’t something I found a major problem on the Enduro 3 when I tested.

These minor upgrades build on Garmin’s best-in-class navigation features, with clear, detailed routable maps you can use to create routes on the fly, or to follow routes sent from the Garmin Connect app.

I find Garmin’s maps clearer to use on the brand’s AMOLED watches, especially in cloudy conditions, but it was still easy to follow routes and use the maps on the Enduro 4.

The Enduro 4 doesn't offer the LTE and satellite connectivity you get on the Fenix 9, or a mic and speaker you can use for voice commands, but it does have Garmin’s other smart features.

These include music storage, the ability to link up with streaming services like Spotify, NFC payments through Garmin Pay, and access to the Connect IQ app store, which is modest in comparison to the App Store or Google Play but contains some useful apps, widgets, watch faces and data fields.

As sports watches go, it’s pretty smart, but it doesn’t have an AMOLED display and if this is a priority for you, then looking at a true smartwatch like the Apple Watch Ultra 4 might be worthwhile, or at least the Fenix 9 Pro and its extra connectivity.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is a reliable, long-lasting adventure watch that’s one of the best options on the market right now if you prefer a MIP display.

It’s more affordable than the Fenix 9 Pro Solar, as well as being lighter and having longer battery life, though you do lose some potentially useful features like the extra connectivity on the Fenix.

The Garmin Enduro 3 offers fierce competition, though. The Enduro 4 isn’t a major update and if you have an older Enduro model and are considering upgrading, I think opting for the cheaper Enduro 3 on sale is a better buy, even if this does run the risk of missing out on some future software updates that only come to the Enduro 4.

If you’re not firmly set on a MIP watch, then I prefer AMOLED devices myself, and it felt like a downgrade to use the Enduro 4 after testing the Fenix 9 Pro and Coros Pace 4 Pro and their brighter displays. The battery life gap between AMOLED and MIP is closing fast, too.

However, I’m pleased to see Garmin maintaining the remaining MIP options within its line-up, because not everyone wants another dazzling AMOLED display in their life, in which case the Enduro 4 is certainly a top option.

#3355. New Apple TV 4K remote’s best feature requires a newer iPhone model

A new Apple TV 4K releases this Friday (pre-order here), with an upgraded Siri Remote. But the new remote’s best feature might not work on your iPhone.

If you’re interested in the new Apple TV 4K launching this week, or perhaps you just want to buy the upgraded Siri Remote separately (available here), there’s a key limitation you should know.

Precision Finding on the new Siri Remote requires an iPhone 17 or newer.

The most common problem with the current Siri Remote is that it’s easy to lose. And once you lose it, Apple doesn’t offer many options for finding it. But that’s changing with the 4th gen Siri Remote.

You can use the new Siri Remote with any previous Apple TV 4K or Apple TV HD model. And if you do, you’ll benefit from the remote’s new built-in speaker that can be triggered from the Find My app.

Joining the new speaker, the other main change with this latest Siri Remote is Precision Finding. If you’ve ever used the Find My app to track down a lost AirTag, you’ll probably be familiar with the feature.

Precision Finding lets you get step-by-step, guided directions that take you directly to the lost Siri Remote. It’s a huge upgrade from the old tool for finding the remote—which mostly just told you that it’s in your house somewhere.

But Precision Finding relies on the Bluetooth 6 support found in iPhone 17 and 17 Pro models (not iPhone 17e), iPhone Air, iPhone Duo, and iPhone 18 Pro models.

So if you don’t have one of those iPhones, you’ll still benefit from the built-in speaker that lets you play a sound to find the lost remote, but Precision Finding won’t be available.

You can buy the new Siri Remote for $59 on Amazon.

Will this limitation impact your Siri Remote purchase decision? Let us know in the comments.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.
