#3330. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

#3326. Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams

How to convince your boss LLMs can’t do it all

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

#3324. End of an era: Apple Support Community forums will permanently close on November 20

Users visiting the Apple Support Community tonight were greeted with a message informing them that the platform will permanently shut down on November 20. Here are the details.

If you have ever had a question or ran into a problem with an Apple product, chances are you have come across the Apple Support Community, the company’s official discussion forums where users from around the world help each other troubleshoot issues and share tips.

The platform has a history dating back to at least 1998, when it was known as Apple Tech Exchange. Since then, it was renamed Apple Discussions before relaunching as Apple Support Communities in April 2011, with a redesigned interface, personalized profiles, and a reputation system that rewarded users for helping others.

Tonight, however, users who tried to access the platform were greeted with the following message:

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.

We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.

Right now, the portal still shows a “Sign in” button, though it leads only to an AppleConnect login page labeled “AC Communities Web – Internal,” suggesting that access is now restricted to Apple employees.

Interestingly, Apple’s message refers to the “AppleCare Support Community,” rather than the “Apple Support Community,” which is how the platform is officially branded.

These forums were often far up when searching for Apple problems, but I’m not sure I ever found a real answer there. So often the threads went no where or someone would link an unhelpful Apple support page.

Still, the forums are already in read-only mode, with users able to browse existing discussions, search for answers, and interact with posts through the “Me too” and voting buttons, but no longer submit new questions or replies.

At the time of writing, the most recent post was published just 57 minutes earlier, suggesting that Apple only recently disabled new submissions.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and clarification on the scope of the shutdown, and we’ll update this story if we hear back.

#3323. The Best, Worst, and Most Surprising Moments of the Latin Grammys

The Latin Grammys never delivers the same show twice, and that was apparent at the 2026 ceremony, which was filled with high highs, low lows, and plenty of surprises.

This year, artists from different genres and regions got some long-awaited recognition, making for heartfelt speeches from first-time winners like Anitta, who took home the award for Best Portuguese Language Contemporary Pop Album after years of creating groundbreaking Brazilian pop. She also used the  moment to highlight her homeland, and remind audiences what the Latin Grammys are all about. Similarly, Milo J celebrated his beloved Argentina as he took home his first trophies last night at just 20 years old, getting some much-deserved praise for his folk-driven album La Vida Era Más Corta.

But for all of the ways the Latin Grammys got it right this year, there were also some hiccups. Here’s some more highlights, misses, and head-scratching moments.

Daddy Yankee cemented his reggaeton royalty status with one of the most exciting performances of the night. The reggaeton pioneer embodied his Person of the Year honor in its entirety as he dove into his classics like “Ella Me Levantó” and “Lo Que Pasó, Pasó.” It may have been a surprise to the audience since Daddy Yankee has shied away from playing his earlier, more party-forward songs since becoming a devout Christian, but he went through all the hits. Daddy Yankee tore into “Rompe” and “Gasolina,” reminding the world of his icon status, and brought out a ton of guests: LL Cool J, French Montana, Diljit Dosanjh, Feid, Bizarrap, Bad Gyal and more. Here’s to hoping he busts out the same set at Coachella — but only if LL Cool J can serve to boisterously remind the world, “Don’t call it a comeback!” —Maya Georgi

Daddy Yankee appeared to pay tribute to Michael Jackson during his show-stopping performance with one white-studded glove on. To the surprise of the audience and everyone watching the Latin Grammys, Janet Jackson appeared a little later to present him with the award for Person of the Year. Daddy Yankee, who looked shock when she walked onstage, previously collaborated with Jackson on her 2018 song “Made For Now.” The king of reggaeton took a moment during his speech to give Ms. Jackson her flowers. “I want to thank you for being here and I respect you a lot,” Daddy Yankee told the icon. —Lucas Villa

Pablo Alborán received a historic 30th Grammy nomination of his career this year. He is the third most-nominated Spanish artist in the history of the Latin Grammy Awards behind Rosalía and Alejandro Sanz. Sadly, the Málaga-based pop star has never won a single Latin Grammy Award. His album KM0 lost to a deluxe edition of Sanz’s ¿Y Ahora Qué? LP. The wild thing is that the original version of Sanz’s album won in the same category last year. After 15 years of Latin Grammy nominations, it was Alborán’s time to finally win and that didn’t happen. —L.V.

Brazilian powerhouse Anitta brought tons of energy to the stage during her show-stopping medley, pulled from her critically acclaimed album EQUILIBRIVM. She glided through “Choka Choka,” “Desgraça,” “Meia Noite,” and “Ouro” from the LP, putting all her star power on display. The performance was a highlight on its own, but the night was even more special for Anitta: The 12-time nominee, who has performed at the ceremony over the years, had never won a trophy  — until now. She scored her first Latin Grammy for Best Portuguese Language Contemporary Pop Album, an honor she dedicated to Brazil while noting how often the country’s culture and contributions are erased from major media moments. “This is the first time a Brazilian category is being televised. It’s very important that you know that Latin America includes all the countries in Latin America, not just the Spanish-speaking one,” she said. “Brazil is part of it.”—Julyssa Lopez

Sure, the rocker has several Grammys under his belt for his work with the Police and beyond, but now the Latin Recording Academy has also recognized String, too. It’s less surprising when you realize Sting won the award for Best Pop/Rock song for his feature on Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso’s song, “Hasta Jesús Tuvo Un Mal Día” from their latest album Free Spirits. Sting had gone on Instagram to explain how he “helped” Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso grapple with their newfound fame during a wellness retreat at a “secretive” holistic Free Spirits Center. We’re not sure if it’s a bit, but either way, the Academy was impressed. —M.G.

Earlier on, before the ceremony’s broadcast kicked off, U.S. representative-elect Bobby Pulido enjoyed a full-circle win and accepted the Best Tejano Album award in person. But besides that non-televised moment, there were practically no speeches or performances that spoke to politics in Latin America or the political realities of Latinos living in the U.S., even from a place of joy for Texas’ big wins in the midterm elections. Last year, Los Tigres del Norte’s performance celebrated immigrants amidst ICE crackdowns. This year, Becky G and Santana’s anti-ICE track was even up for Song of the Year. So it’s not unprecedented for the ceremony to veer into current events. It was strange for an award show broadcast live from Las Vegas, and stranger still for a night dedicated to celebrating Latin voices. —M.G.

Milo J has been one of Argentina’s most exciting newcomers, particularly for the way he incorporates tradition with modern sounds. He put that on display on Thursday with a touching performance that nodded to the customs of Santiago del Estero, a city he has deep connections to that inspired his album La Vida Era Más Corta. He transformed the stage into a traditional courtyard from the region and brought on musician Gustavo Santaolalla and the Uruguayan ensemble Agárrate Catalina for “Solifican12” and “Gil.” The effect was impressive and emotional, and a testament to why he scored three Latin Grammys that night. —J.L.

One of this year’s biggest breakthrough artists took home the award for Best New Artist and it felt right. Aria Vega, the rising pop star from Barranquilla, emerged victorious in a category with 10 other artists this year. Vega has scored hit after hit embracing the sounds of Colombia’s Caribbean coast in songs “Chévere” and “Cule Poco.” She previously told Rolling Stone, “I want people to see us beyond the stereotypes and experience the coast through my eyes. If I can make somebody curious about where I’m from, or make someone from back home feel proud to see themselves reflected in what I do, that means everything to me.” —L.V.

What was going on with the music during the award packages? No award show gets it perfectly, but this year’s Latin Grammys seemed to be struggling to let audiences at home hear the songs that were nominated for several categories. The sound glitched out during the Best Contemporary Tropical Album category and then audio issues seemed to pop up throughout the telecast. The worst was when they hit a few of the speeches, including Rosalia’s heartfelt words when she won Best Pop Song for “La Perla.” —J.L.

Before they broke up, Karol G and Feid teamed up for the song “Verano Rosa” on last year’s Tropicoqueta album. The song was nominated for Best Reggaeton Performance. To possibly avoid an awkward moment during the telecast, “Verano Rosa” was announced as the winner in the category during the pre-show ceremony. To no one’s surprise, neither Karol G nor Feid were present to accept the award. Feid now shares his two Latin Grammy wins with Bad Bunny and his former partner, Karol G. Still, it’s a nice nod to the way they were and the solid collaborations that came out that partnership. —L.V.

This year’s Latin Grammy Awards was packed with performances from start to finish. You would forget they were giving out awards from the few that were broadcasted during the telecast. (Actually, a majority of the awards are handed out in a pre-telecast ceremony.) On top of a show bloated with performance, there were a few that went on for too long. If you’re going to have an award ceremony filled with performances, let’s cut out the filler. —L.V.

Just days after he won his competitive race in Texas’ 15th congressional district, Bobby Pulido kept on triumphing by taking the Latin Grammys stage. On Thursday, the Tejano musician took home the trophy for Best Tejano Album for his project Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol. 2/En Vivo). This marked his third Latin Grammy; he won his first Latin Grammy in 2022 for Best Tejano Album for his LP Para Que Baile Mi Pueblo and his second in 2025 for Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol. 1/En Vivo). But as he accepted the award, he was quick to remind people that what’s important to him now is his commitment to public service. “I love you all, and I’ll see you soon, because we need to represent and we need to get to work to use our voices for something else,” he said. —J.L.

#3322. Reddit Reviews goes against the whole philosophy of the platform, say users

Many Redditors have expressed dismay at the launch of Reddit Reviews, a new AI-powered feature which aims to summarise posts about particular products.

Reddit is positioning the feature as a way to save time and effort when researching a potential purchase, but many Redditors say that replacing human interaction with AI summaries is antithetical to the whole philosophy of the platform – and is going to make the existing spam problem massively worse …

The value of customer reviews on ecommerce platforms like Amazon is becoming increasingly questionable thanks to practices like astroturfing by brands and offering people free products in return for five-star reviews.

That’s led to Reddit becoming one of the most trusted sources of feedback and advice on potential purchases, precisely because it’s a forum in which real people are free to express their true opinions. Indeed, many use a filter in their Google searches to draw content from Reddit specifically, adding the suffix ‘site:reddit.com’.

Reddit is increasingly a cesspool of maligned moderators (human and bot) and owners looking to make a bot. Posters on the platform are simply supplying free content with nothing to gain except bans when someone/somebot disagrees with them.

Reddit certainly isn’t immune to astroturfing – that is, fake posts by brands posing as ordinary users – but moderators put a lot of work into deleting spam and other inauthentic posts.

The platform yesterday announced the launch of Reddit Reviews, in which AI summarises the posts made about particular products and product categories. It’s being pitched as a way for people to save time when seeking the product opinions of Redditors.

Across Reddit’s communities, people discuss everything from hobbies and daily life to products they’re researching. By offering perspectives grounded in real experience, these conversations provide valuable context in every purchase decision journey […]

Today, we are starting to test Reddit Reviews, a new experience that organizes product conversations from across Reddit into dedicated reviews and highlights the most important takeaways from across our communities.

However, as CNET spotted, the move has led to a backlash by many Redditors and subreddit moderators.

“I’ve already seen this in practice and it is a nightmare. It turns a basic conversation into an ad-ridden distracting mess. It’s horrible to read and had me fleeing every thread I saw it in.”

“I am a moderator on a couple of health subs and we explicitly do not allow advertisements because most of them are bullshit slop and completely predatory for vulnerable and newly diagnosed patients. We do not want, or need this, on our subs!”

“Yeah, this definitely isn’t going to lead to even more fake account stealth marketing efforts across the site.”

“This is going to make our spam fighting even worse. This is horrible.”

“Every decision made by Reddit lately encourages spam and/or abuse that will make spam.”

“Not a single person who uses Reddit wants this.”

“You are incentivising existing spammers to continue or step up their activities, now that there’s a new well they can poison.”

I find it hard to disagree with the view that almost every monetization step the platform has made has degraded the user experience. This seems almost guaranteed to be another one.

#3321. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3320. ‘The Body’ Was Meant to Be Dark. Geena Meszaros Also Makes It Hilarious

Maybe it’s fortune. Maybe it’s fate. Maybe something a bit more mystical. But actress Geena Meszaros still truly believes it was a stroke of unimaginable luck that landed her the breakout role of Lisbeth in Netflix’s newest teen horror-comedy The Body. Mostly because she didn’t realize she was trying out for one of the show’s leads.

Meszaros was given partial scripts during much of the audition process, which kept some of the story’s big twists and turns opaque. “I managed to go through the callback and chemistry reads without knowing how integral [Lisbeth] was to the story,” Meszaros says, laughing on a Zoom from her Calgary home. But the more she found out as the process went along, “I was obsessed.”

Created by Quinn Shephard (Not Okay, Under the Bridge), The Body drops viewers into the dramas of a small-town all-girls Catholic high school sometime around 2004 (you can tell because the cell phones click closed and they’re using AIM). The dance team, queens of the school’s social order, has to fill a single spot on the roster, and captain Anya Butler (Kristina Bogic) and her right hand Elise Zakaria (Sara Boustany) pick the fresh-faced and pious “Saint” Grace Franklin (Sofia Wylie) over the stiff-limbed outcast Lisbeth Anderson, played by Meszaros. But the team initiation ceremony — a tongue-in-cheek sacrament of Ecstasy and a warm bottle of Tanqueray representing the body and blood of Satan — goes awry, ending with Grace unresponsive. In the aftermath, Anya and Lisbeth are bonded by a dark secret about what happened that night, and the town slowly succumbs to a wave of religious hysteria.

“Lisbeth starts as an outsider. She [views] these girls’ friendships as a commodity. She’s a survivalist, in a way,” Meszaros says. “She sees the power Anya has because of the [team’s] group think. And she slowly realizes that she needs it to maintain her safety. She has to get a taste.”  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

This isn’t Meszaros’ first time tackling a spiritual conundrum. Fans of Mae Martin’s  conversion-camp horror series Wayward might recognize Meszaros, who played the offputting Oatmeal Beth. But The Body puts Meszaros front and center, her character driving much of the action. With Grace in a coma, Anya lets Lisbeth take her place on the dance team. But it’s clear from the jump that she’s the misfit of the group. Meszaros’ pale face and wide-eyed expressions comically clash with the rest of the girls’ perfect blowouts, makeup, and headbands. She’s so disconnected from normal teenager stuff — shopping, flirting, texting — that much of what she says is laugh-out-loud obtuse, lighting some of the horrific elements of the series with dark humor. The series also reveals that Lisbeth’s family moved to the town after the mysterious death of her father — baggage she’s desperate to keep from her new friends.

When Shephard started casting The Body, she tells Rolling Stone, it was imperative that the character of Lisbeth be “unnerving in a way she cannot shake,” no matter how much she imitates and studies the popular girls around her. What surprised her was how Meszaros took what was written to be unsettling and also made it funny, turning Lisbeth into an “adorable maniac.”

“Lisbeth cannot speak the same language they speak, struggles to read social cues, is deeply traumatized by her childhood, and is sheltered enough to misunderstand most pop-culture references. Watching Lisbeth is like watching someone on their first day on Earth,” Shephard says. “There was really no one else who had the level of humor that Geena brought to this. She is so absurdly funny.”

The show manages a blend of high drama and comedy reminiscent of some of the most outrageous episodes of Euphoria — helped along by delightful appearances by Traitors star Gabby Windey as the dance team’s heavily pregnant Coach Miller. (“Every time I came to set and saw her fake belly sitting in its little bucket in the makeup room, I was like, ‘Oh, yeah, it’s gonna be a good day.’” Meszaros says, chuckling. “What an icon.”) Related Content Netflix to Release Documentary ‘Russell Brand: Open Secret’ Angie Martinez’s Unaired Tupac Shakur Interview Set for Release After 30 Years Jennie Celebrates Sisterhood on Anthemic Pop Single ‘Someone to Hold’ 'Possible Love' Is a Tragedy, a Timebomb — and the Best Movie of 2026

Lisbeth’s attempt to win over the team gets complicated when the girls start seeing visions of Grace, which often compel them to loudly repent their sins. And when people in the town start believing Grace is a real-life saint, a spiritual frenzy spreads through the community, Contagion-style. Amid the chaos, Lisbeth clings more tightly to the secret of her own past trauma, and soon the quiet wallflower cracks open onscreen, revealing a manipulative streak and mysterious religious power. Yet, Lisbeth’s underlying motivation rings achingly familiar: Sure, the town is slowly crumbling under the weight of a witch hunt-esque fever. But wouldn’t it be great if Lisbeth could stay popular?

“When you get to high school, you’re really trying to figure out who you are, sans parents,” Meszaros says. “It’s such an influential time. For me, I’ve always been someone that molds to the people I’m around. Especially as a teenager, you’re going through all these changes, you’re [always] embarrassed, and people are at different stages. Being a teenager is hard, man. It’s hard.”

In addition to obvious nods to films like Jennifer’s Body, The Crucible, The Craft, and But I’m a Cheerleader, the show clearly takes inspiration from the Bible. Anya, Lisbeth, and Grace make a kind of  Holy Trinity: Anya as the benevolent father, Lisbeth as a savior rejected by the people she’s come to help, and Grace as the silent but ever-present Holy Spirit. The dynamic underscores the show’s themes about questioning one’s faith. Specifically for Lisbeth, the question stops being about what she believes and rather if she wants to believe at all.

“There’s moments where certain people who are devout are triggering [for Lisbeth], because [that’s] a version of herself that she feels like she lost,” Meszaros says. “She’s questioning her faith. And losing that stability, she sees the world as like a place where you have to have your own back. It’s skewed. It’s extreme. And it’s a huge driving factor for the choices she makes. She’s hypervigilant — and she’s always wary that something could go wrong.”  Trending Stories Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage John Mulaney Has Many Thoughts on the 2026 Rock Hall Inductees — And Picks Next Year’s Class The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Dolly Parton Heals the Soul on Final Recording, ‘Torn,’ a Duet With Bono on U2’s New Album

Meszaros is careful to leave many of the series’ central mysteries and twists up to audience interpretation. But the one thing she’s clear about is how protective she’s feeling of Lisbeth and the emotions welling up from releasing her first big character into the world.

“If you have to judge her, I understand. She does some questionable things, for sure,” Meszaros says. “But I’m still Team Lisbeth.”

#3318. Keychron just ended the magnetic vs. mechanical keyboard debate: the V6 Ultra Hybrid proves you can have both with literally no compromises and even a magnetic tactile switch

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Someone had to do dual MX/HE compatibility properly, and Keychron stepped up to the mark. The Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE offers dual magnetic and mechanical switch compatibility, plus the widest array of magnetic hot-swappability I’ve yet seen. It’s formidable for gaming, beautiful for typing, built well and reasonably priced. It’s a little bland-looking, but that’s a minor point, and we had a small QC issue, although I’d expect that to be fixed in full production units.

Minor QC issues (hopefully fixed by full production)

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE (catchy name, right?) attempts to forge ‘The One Ring’ of keyboards. One keyboard to rule them all, to do and be everything for everyone. The master keyboard.

As such, it’s the latest in a very small selection of keyboards that offer dual mechanical and magnetic capability. If you want to hot-swap from magnetic back to mechanical switches, you can. But the V6 takes things further with, as I alluded to above, an altogether more holistic approach. The V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE also packs everything else Keychron has to throw at a keyboard — which essentially means every feature that actually exists right now.

8K polling, tons of magnetic features and customization in the Launcher app, gasket mounting for comfortable typing — all with a reasonable price tag. It also offers my holy grail feature at checkout: a magnetic and tactile switch, for elite gaming and typing without even needing to hot-swap in the first place.

So, like, is this legitimately the perfect hybrid board? The best gaming keyboard and the best mechanical keyboard all rolled into one? I think so. Keychron has done it. Find out more in my full Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE review.

Where to even start? Proper MX/HE hot swap, bags of gaming and productivity performance, reasonable price — this is a Goldilocks keyboard.

The V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE’s main feature is denoted by the “Hybrid” part of its (terribly convoluted) name. This board is dual mechanical/magnetic switch compatible, meaning you can swap between the two.

The V6 Ultra Hybrid takes any standard 3-pin or 5-pin mechanical switches. It also supports a wide range of magnetic switches with the N Pole facing downwards — that means Gateron x Wooting Jade switches, Gateron KS-20 switches, and any of Gateron’s ever-growing line of dual rail magnetic switches. Neat.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Now Keychron isn’t the first to do dual MX/HE. Glorious did it a while back with the hilariously overpriced GMMK 3 HE. More recently, Lofree had a pop with the Hyzen, but with typically Lofree results: great looks and typing but rank amateurism in the software department (pivotal to a magnetic board). Keychron, in usual Keychron fashion, is the first to do a proper job of it, with the widest magnetic hot-swap scope while still keeping things affordable.

The long and short is that the V6 Ultra Hybrid has more actual hot-swap potential than any other magnetic board that I know of. Most magnetic boards claim to be hot swappable, but only support a couple of switch variants from the same specific magnetic switch line — often the variants available at checkout. In reality, that usually makes hot-swap claims severely hamstrung at best; meaningless at worst. Not so here. Again, the Lofree Hyzen also supports an impressive roster of compatible magnetic switches, but lacks the professional polish of Keychron’s boards.

The “hybrid” moniker also has another related meaning. The V6 Ultra Hybrid is a hybrid board for both work and play, offering powerful gaming performance while capable enough to handle the rigors of work and heavy typing.

The bit that excites me most are two of the magnetic switch choices available from stock. The V6 Ultra Hybrid ships with one of four Gateron Ultra Fast Lime magnetic switches, two of which are tactile. Yes, tactile magnetic switches — this is the biggest news in my opinion.

All magnetic switches up to now have been linear in operation. Sure, being able to hot-swap those is fine, but swapping out 108 switches from a full-sized keyboard is a ginormous time suck. So it’s not like you can just quickly switch from tactiles for work to magnetic for gaming. If, like me, you enjoy tactile switches but want magnetic gaming performance, you’ve so far been left out in the cold. Not anymore.

The V6 Ultra Hybrid also packs plenty of Keychron’s productivity heritage. There’s a gasket mount, for bouncy and comfortable typing; Keychron’s steeply-raked and deeply-sculpted OSA profile keycaps, which I find ideal for fast typing; and screw-in stabilizers for minimal big key wobble. As you can see, my typing speed and accuracy were both above average on the V6 Ultra Hybrid, helped by paring back the actuation to 2.6mm — my personal sweet spot and where I type-test all magnetic boards. I could (and indeed did) type on this thing all day.

Thanks to Gateron’s magnetic switches, you also get every elite gaming feature under the sun right now: adjustable actuation; rapid trigger; dynamic keystroke for multiple commands per actuation; custom SOCD resolutions for last key prioritization (A.K.A. ‘Snap Tap’). There’s 8K polling too, although on a keyboard this is tantamount to snake oil, if you ask me. All of this is customizable through Keychron’s fantastic web launcher.

I used the board for everything, from competitive gaming on “Counter-Strike 2” and “Wardogs,” through to more relaxed titles like “Total War: Rome II,” “Valheim,” and “Dune: Awakening.” It never put a foot wrong.

Admittedly, if you want a board purely for competitive FPS gaming, you’re probably better off with a plate-, tray-, or top-mounted magnetic board like the NuPhy Air60 HE, NuPhy Field75 HE, or Keychron Q16 HE 8K — these mount styles aren’t as comfortable, but move around less than a gasket mount, making them less likely to cause accidental inputs at super low <0.5mm switch actuations.

If you need an all-rounder for both work and play, though, I seriously can’t think of a better board than the V6 Ultra Hybrid.

As this is a Keychron board, you get all the expected goodies. Aside from some QC issues I’ll cover later, the board is built well, using premium materials. The case is sturdy ABS plastic with very little bend and flex — impressive given this is a long board.

The keycaps are doubleshot PBT, which will stand up well to wear and tear without going shiny, unlike ABS keycaps. PBT is also grease resistant. I did my usual test, typing on the keyboard after eating Monster Munch (a fried corn snack here in the U.K.), and the V6’s keycaps picked up a lot of grease but were easy to wipe down. Not quite as impressive as the caps on the Logitech G Pro X2 Rapid, which completely resisted the same grease altogether — like not even a single smear.

The V6 features a decent 4,000mAh battery, plus triple Bluetooth, 2.4G and wired connectivity, toggleable via a switch on the case. There’s a macOS/Windows toggle, too, but Keychron still supplies separate sets of Windows and macOS command keys rather than dual-labeling its keycaps. This is a longstanding frustration of mine. I switch between the two OS’ constantly for work. It’s great to have the toggle, but it undermines the ease if I have to switch keycaps too. A small issue, but one that’s so easily solvable by dual labelling — as proved by the Lofree Hyzen and Lofree Flow 2.

When I reviewed the original Keychron V6, which I awarded a full five stars, one of my favorite features was the price. It offered major performance for a very reasonable sum. The V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE is pricier. It costs $164 versus the $99 basic V6 and the $119 V6 Ultra (which has faster polling, better internal damping, nicer switches, etc — just an all-round upgraded package).

However, the V6 Ultra Hybrid packs a lot more functionality than the lower-tier V6 models thanks to the dual MX/HE switch compatibility, and way more gaming features when using HE switches. An extra $45 over the standard V6 Ultra is fair game for all that, at least in my book.

Let’s look at the hybrid MX/HE competition, too. The Lofree Hyzen costs a whopping $279 — sure it’s made from aluminum and is beautiful to behold, but the software is janky as hell. The Glorious GMMK 3 HE starts at $179, but you can easily get up to near $500 for choice productivity upgrades (and to make it look less ugly than stock). By those two yardsticks, the V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE is the best value-for-money hybrid board on the market, and it ain’t even close.

At the time of writing, the V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE is in pre-order, after its Kickstarter campaign, with estimated shipping starting December 2026.

As I’ve mentioned in previous reviews, I absolutely hate that Keychron floats its new boards on Kickstarter. Keychron is a major keyboard brand (arguably the dominant productivity market force) that absolutely does not need to crowdfund its boards. Besides, as someone who has tested several of Keychron’s crowdfunded boards, I can tell you they’re already developed and practically finished by the start of the campaigns (because most Keychron boards are 95% the same under the hood). Oh well. That’s just unfortunately how Keychron chooses to operate, but you can rest assured that there’s usually very little chance of a crowdfunding rug pull from this brand.

There’s very little I don’t like about the V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE, aside from its ridiculously long-winded name. It’s a little boring to look at, I guess, and I saw some QC teething issues, but nothing that should seriously dissuade you.

Ah, look: black plastic case, gray rounded keycaps, a tiny bit of color on the ESC key. It must be a Keychron! Yawn. I’m not saying the V6 Ultra Hybrid is bad-looking, but it’s the same old Keychron design we’ve seen for years now. And it’s getting kinda boring.

Now, as someone who has owned, tested, used, or edited the reviews of literally hundreds of keyboards, this probably affects me more than you. I see a lot of Keychrons; you’ll probably only see the one you buy.

But man, I wish Keychron would make some more exciting decks in its more affordable V- and K-series sometimes. Pretty boards with plenty of color, like the NuPhy Halo75; or handsome futuristic designs like the Lofree Hyzen and Lofree Block. Come on, Keychron, spice it up a bit.

As Keychron has grown, I’ve seen firsthand its once stellar reputation for build quality start to drop. A few years ago, every single Keychron board we tested was built like a tank. Now we’re seeing frequent issues with sticky switches or other build quality concerns. Not all the time, I must say. And Keychron is always keen to hear from us when this happens, so we always tell its representatives and receive a replacement in quick order. But it’s getting to the point now that I’m seeing a pattern I can’t ignore.

My first V6 Ultra Hybrid review unit suffered both a sticky switch (solved by adjusting debounce time) and a USB dongle port that was far too large with no magnet inside, meaning the 2.4G receiver would fall out. Keychron’s representative has assured me this was a pre-production teething issue, and issued me a full production unit where the problem has been fixed. But as I said above, similar issues are becoming too common now from this once wholly reliable brand, and it’s a problem I need to call out. Keychron, if you’re reading, please step your game back up.

I utterly adore this keyboard. I won’t be using it long-term because I prefer a 75% layout (so I‘m eagerly waiting for a V2 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE). But I absolutely love what this deck signifies.

As is so often the case in the productivity keyboard arena, it takes Keychron to turn its attention to an innovation to truly bring that feature into the mainstream and make it work. Dual MX/HE compatibility is now here, with proper wide-ranging switch support for both mechanical and magnetic. And there’s a tactile magnetic switch on offer to boot.

If you want one keyboard that excels for literally every purpose, without breaking the bank, it’s the Keychron V6 Ultra Hybrid 8K HE. End of story.

Ralph Earle joined the IBM Software Lab in Raleigh, N.C., in 1990 as a technical editor and retired as a senior software engineer in 2017. #3316. This video lets you actually see the ‘incredible’ new MacBook Pro cooling system

When Apple launched the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, the company said that it had completely redesigned the cooling system for “incredible sustained performance.”

That could sound like marketing hype, but a YouTuber has found a great way to let us actually see the new system living up to Apple’s claims …

The real-life performance of any electronic device depends not only on the power of the chip but a range of additional factors. A key one is the effectiveness of the cooling system, because when the device gets too hot, the performance will be throttled in order to avoid damage.

In the worst of cases, the theoretical maximum performance of a chip is only delivered for a very short time before it is throttled back to a much lower level. Thermal management is absolutely key in the case of a laptop like the MacBook Pro.

Apple said that the latest model has a completely new cooling system.

A completely redesigned thermal architecture enables […] incredible sustained performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, even in a lighter design, while redirecting warm air away from the display.

As Macworld spotted, a YouTuber has found a simple but clever way to enable us to actually see the difference with our own eyes.

A YouTube video by Geekerwan compared the mini-LED MacBook Pro with the new PROLED XDR model using a fog machine. With each MacBook’s fans running, you can clearly see how the internal design disperses the heat: In the old model, heat goes both out and up through the display, while the PROLED pushes the heat toward the back of the device through the hinge.

Cooling is particularly challenging when the laptop is closed while connected to an external monitor, and the results of the testing show a dramatic improvement by the latest model. You can watch the video below, which links directly to the demo – but Geekerwan’s videos are always worth watching in full, so click here to watch the whole thing.

#3315. Trump’s Cabinet Is in Disarray Over Nvidia’s Honeypot Disaster

There’s a bitter war over trade policy underway in the back rooms of the Trump administration that pivots on an unlikely fulcrum: one tech CEO’s inability to keep it in his pants.

By now, you’ve likely heard about Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, one of the largest makers of the chips and technology powering the economic juggernaut of artificial intelligence. Huang was forced to resign earlier this week after the shocking revelation that he had been having an extramarital affair with a woman named Alice Huang — no relation — who U.S. intelligence services think is an asset for the Chinese government. Until his resignation, Huang was one of the most important CEOs in the country, presiding over the world’s most valuable company. He sat near Trump at a state dinner with China in September, and basically had the president on speed-dial.

But where the various money men in Trump’s Cabinet get involved has to do with the mistress, Alice Huang, who also happened to be the leader of a Singaporean company called Megaspeed that was buying up Nvidia chips as fast as it could get them.

The New York Times reports that the Treasury, Defense, and State departments all wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist for months — even before the Huang honeypot affair had broken — but they weren’t the ones who made the final call. No, that particular blacklist is handled by the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick. Lutnick has been more of a dove when it comes to sanctions policy, advocating against big, broad export restrictions that would, say, block the sale of AI chips to a shell company for the Chinese intelligence services, but also gum up the works for various other countries. And on Nvidia specifically, Lutnik has basically been a trusty friend. The Times also reports that, like Trump, Lutnick has a personal relationship with Huang and has repeatedly gone easy on him when it comes to trade policy decisions like this.

All of that appears to have royally pissed off the other big money man in Trump’s Cabinet: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department had been trying to get Commerce to blacklist Megaspeed for months. This conflict came to a head, Axios reports, in a direct confrontation between the two men in the Situation Room on the Thursday after the midterm elections, after which Lutnick said he would “look into it.” Axios reports that other officials had repeatedly warned one of Lutnick’s deputies, undersecretary Jeff Kessler, about Megaspeed’s risks before the Situation Room clash. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Bessent publicly addressed the issue on Friday. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent said on CNBC this morning, referring to the Commerce Department refusing to blacklist Megaspeed, effectively throwing Lutnick under the bus. “The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?”

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blames Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Nvidia chip mess: "Treasury, War, USTR and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months." pic.twitter.com/0BTlHymwUY

Lutnik appears to understand that his role in the Nvidia fallout is going to come under scrutiny. A spokesperson told CNN on Friday that the Secretary had “proactively agreed” to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee in Congress – which means he will have to face some of these questions directly in the near future.   Trending Stories Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage John Mulaney Has Many Thoughts on the 2026 Rock Hall Inductees — And Picks Next Year’s Class The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For Dolly Parton Heals the Soul on Final Recording, ‘Torn,’ a Duet With Bono on U2’s New Album

The second part of Bessent’s quote, though, is part of a big question that administration officials are probably asking: How much did Huang or his people know? Did the guy who was calling up Trump onstage at tech conferences know he was sleeping with and selling advanced AI chips to a Chinese spy? It’s not as if Megaspeed’s business was particularly subtle. The Times reports that the company was buying Nvidia’s chips and using them to set up data centers in Southeast Asia that would service Chinese companies, skirting U.S. export controls. The U.S. government was also looking into the company for literally smuggling some of the chips into China directly, which seems like the kind of thing the CEO of Nvidia should have maybe been aware of before he started sleeping with Megaspeed’s top executive.

Alas, the heart wants what it wants. Scott Bessent’s heart, we can presume, really wants to hit Lutnick over the head with a folding chair. Alice Huang’s heart, it seems, wanted to successfully skirt U.S. regulations on behalf of the Chinese tech industry. And Jensen Huang, well, he just wanted to smooch women and look good in a leather jacket — and it turns out, he had the chips to do that all along.

#3314. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3313. I feel a little nostalgic about the Apple Support Community forums, but it was time

Yesterday brought a surprise move by Apple when it abruptly ceased write access to the Apple Support Community and announced that it would be permanently closing in just over a week.

While the news does make me a little nostalgic, I do have to say that I think its time had long since come and gone …

As we noted yesterday, the community has a fairly long history. It started in 1998 as the Apple Tech Exchange before being renamed Apple Discussions and finally relaunching as Apple Support Communities in 2011. There were some paid community specialists working for Apple on the forum, while the majority of the responses came from volunteers.

The company’s statement was brief and didn’t give any official explanation for the shutdown.

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

Interestingly, Verizon did exactly the same thing with its own Community Forum earlier this year, with an immediate switch to read-only access, followed shortly afterwards by closing it altogether. That too had a reasonably long history, having first launched back in 2008.

I suspect in both cases this was mostly about streamlining operations and reducing costs. CEO John Ternus does seem to be aiming to improve efficiency and eliminate what he views as unnecessary expenses. Additionally, community forums always run the risk of reputational damage when customers criticize decisions made by the company.

I’m old enough to remember the times when the forum was one of the first places I’d turn when troubleshooting an issue with an Apple product, but in all honesty, that hasn’t been the case for a very long time now. A lot of the suggestions were very basic steps any experienced user would already have tried.

There was sometimes also a snarky tone to some of the responses, essentially amounting to “Apple doesn’t promise you should be able to do X, so why are you expecting to do this?” or “Apple already provides a better way to do Y so use it.”

If you were very new to Apple devices and needed very basic help, then I’m sure it could sometimes prove useful, but I have to say that for a very long time now my own starting point has always been Reddit. I don’t think too many people are going to mourn the passing of ASC.

#3311. WhatsApp may soon replace the Communities tab on iOS

Some WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are seeing a new option in the app’s bottom navigation bar that replaces the Communities tab. Here are the details.

Over the past few years, WhatsApp has increasingly focused on Communities as more people have turned to messaging platforms to interact in smaller, more private groups rather than through traditional social networks.

At the same time, WhatsApp has been testing several features that make it easier for users to see which of their contacts are online and available to chat.

Back in May, WABetaInfo found that WhatsApp was developing a new Contacts hub that would bring together users’ favorite contacts, as well as those who were currently online or had recently been active.

A few weeks later, WhatsApp began testing a new green dot indicator on iOS to make it easier to identify contacts who were online.

Now, WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is rolling out the new Contacts hub to some iOS beta testers, replacing the Communities tab in the app’s bottom navigation bar.

The new tab includes a section with favorite contacts and a full contact list. Users can see their favorite contacts at the top of the screen, making it easier to start a conversation with them. They can also sort the full contact list by activity, alphabetical, and birthdays. With alphabetical, the app organizes contacts by name. With activity, WhatsApp shows who is currently online at the top of the list. WhatsApp marks these contacts with a green dot, so users can easily distinguish them from offline contacts. WhatsApp also sorts recently active contacts by last seen, so users can quickly identify who was active most recently. With birthdays, WhatsApp sorts contacts by their upcoming birthday, so users can see who has a birthday coming up soon.

The site notes that the new tab also allows users to add contacts directly, with the option to sync them to their iPhone’s address book.

As for Communities, the feature itself isn’t going away, but rather being moved to a dedicated filter in the Chats tab.

WABetaInfo also notes that WhatsApp is experimenting with potentially replacing the Updates tab, rather than Communities, with the Contacts tab in a future configuration.

For now, the new Contacts tab is available to a limited number of beta testers running the latest WhatsApp beta for iOS via TestFlight, with a broader rollout expected over the coming weeks.
